Job description 
The Netherlands targets using only sustainable energy by 2050, yet 161 offshore oil and gas facilities are still active. Integrating renewables into their daily operation during phase-out can reduce environmental impact but introduces additional uncertainty, requiring costly and time-consuming implementation of new controllers as existing infrastructure is already equipped with functioning control structures. The central question now is: How can we enable practical implementation of optimization-based control in offshore energy systems with integrated renewables by building on existing control infrastructure?
Control systems in energy-intensive industries are designed to meet three goals: satisfy demand, ensure quality, and maintain safety. The ability to meet the goals combined with simplicity of implementation have been decisive factors when developing classic control systems, with environmental impact treated as an afterthought. Data-based controllers use advanced optimization algorithms to achieve these goals and meet environmental constraints. However, the complex mathematics involved makes them far from straightforward to implement in real-world infrastructure. This project aims to propose new adaptation methods for operating offshore facilities by merging online data-driven modelling to capture degradation of equipment over time with optimization-based methods to facilitate the transition to energy neutrality.
The PhD would join the group of Dr Marta Zagorowska at Delft Center for Systems and Control (DCSC) and work together with other researchers in the area of advanced process control systems.
Teaching activities are part of your PhD trajectory and may include, for example: supervising workgroups or lab sessions, assisting in courses, or mentoring BSc and MSc students. While teaching will not be your main responsibility, it offers valuable experience that supports your development and prepares you for future academic or professional roles. Teaching activities will not exceed 20% of your total appointment, averaged over the course of your PhD.

The ideal candidate will be an ambitious, proactive, reflective, and results-driven researcher. We are looking for the following:

When people feel threatened, they react by fight, flight, or freeze. Strikingly, freeze is often overlooked in therapy, although it is strongly linked to poor recovery from mental health conditions. Moreover, little is known about how fight–flight–freeze reactions unfold over time. This project maps how patients with personality disorders move between defensive reactions in daily life and treatment, identifies maladaptive patterns, and examines key underlying mechanisms. 
 Your job

You will design studies, coordinate data collection at Altrecht Center for Personality Disorders, and analyse longitudinal EMA data collected both during psychotherapy sessions and in daily life. You will collaborate with therapists and patients through focus groups to define meaningful indicators of defensive states and to ensure clinical relevance throughout the project.  You will test proof-of-principle freeze-targeted interventions and contribute to the development of state-specific clinical guidelines. You will also write scientific articles and contribute to dissemination activities. Throughout the project, you will work in close collaboration with a PhD candidate at the Methods and Statistics department, for example on complex data analysis, and the development of personalised visualisations for use by clinicians and patients.
 You also contribute to teaching activities within the Department of Clinical Psychology (approximately 10% of your appointment).
 Your qualities
 A (Research) Master level diploma in Clinical Psychology or a related education
 Excellent mastery of English, and good writing skills
 Interest in (and preferably experience with) longitudinal or intensive longitudinal data
 Interest in innovative statistical methods (i.e., Hidden Markov Models)
 Experience with statistical software (for example R)
 Affinity with clinical populations

 An ambition for high quality research
 The ability to work at the interface of science and clinical practice
 Good social and organisational skills, preferably with experience in (coordinating) data collection

 Preserving and restoring agricultural sustainability in Europe requires a monitoring framework quantifying how single and combined agricultural management practices affect European soil ecosystem services. The project aims to develop site specific recommendations for the implementation of agricultural practices in arable farming systems that enhance their contribution to a sustainable environment. The project is part of an ongoing European research project with 17 research partners. By finetuning and extending existing regional soil health assessment frameworks to assess the integrative contribution of crop, soil, nutrient and water management practices, this project will deliver new knowledge to enable farmers and policy makers to improve the ecosystem services the soil supplies, and to enable decision-makers to explore scenario outcomes, assess impacts and incorporate the results into soil quality related policy recommendations at national and EU level.

What new physics emerges when a THz interface changes on the timescale of the wave itself? 
In this PhD project, you will develop dynamically modulated THz interfaces and explore frequency conversion, beam steering, and nonreciprocal propagation through electromagnetic design, device development, and THz experiments.
 Information 
The sub-THz regime is emerging as an important platform for future wireless communication, radar, and sensing, but controlling these waves dynamically remains a major challenge. Current interfaces can shape a THz wave in space, or tune their response in time, but doing both rapidly and with subwavelength spatial control is much harder. This limits how quickly THz beams can be steered, reconfigured, or made nonreciprocal.
In this PhD project, you will explore a different regime: space–time interfaces whose electromagnetic response changes while the wave is interacting with them. Fast modulation allows the interface to exchange energy and momentum with the field, enabling effects such as frequency conversion, dynamic beam steering, anomalous scattering, and nonreciprocal propagation.
Your research will span the full cycle from concept to experiment. You will:
 Develop concepts for fast spatial and temporal modulation of THz waves.
 Model wave interactions with dynamically changing interfaces.
 Design structures combining subwavelength spatial control with high modulation rates.
 Explore suitable modulation mechanisms, including MEMS-based architectures and alternative dynamic platforms.
 Fabricate and experimentally characterize the resulting devices.
 Build THz experiments to study beam steering, frequency shifts, and nonreciprocal response.
 Demonstrate GHz-rate two-dimensional spatiotemporal beamforming and explore its use in reconfigurable and nonreciprocal THz communication.
The project will primarily target the sub-THz regime, approximately 0.3–1 THz. MEMS-based structures are one promising route, but the broader goal is to identify and realize practical platforms that can modulate THz waves fast enough to access genuinely dynamic wave phenomena.
The project is part of SPARK – Spatiotemporal Photonic Technologies, a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Network bringing together academic and industrial partners across Europe. You will be based at Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e) and supervised by Dr. Ahmed H. Dorrah, with Prof. Michaël Lobet at Université de Namur, Belgium, as co-supervisor.
At TU/e, you will join the Photonics and Semiconductor Nanophysics (PSN) group, working in an interdisciplinary environment spanning photonics, electromagnetics, structured waves, nanofabrication, and experimental optics.
You will spend 6 months at Université de Namur, focusing on theoretical modelling of GHz space–time interfaces, and 3 months at TNO, working on THz mode (de)multiplexing and system-level characterization. You will also take part in SPARK training schools, workshops, conferences, and network-wide activities.

ADDITIONAL INFORMATION:
Benefits A meaningful job in a dynamic and ambitious university, in an interdisciplinary setting and within an international network. You will work on a beautiful, green campus at the heart of one of Europe’s largest tech hubs.
In addition, we offer you:
 Full-time employment for four years, with an intermediate assessment after nine months. 
 You will spend a minimum of 10% of your four-year employment on teaching tasks, with a maximum of 15% per year of your employment.
 Salary and benefits (such as a pension scheme, paid pregnancy and maternity leave, partially paid parental leave) in accordance with the Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Universities , scale P (min. € 3,204 - max. € 4,051 gross base salary per month (full-time)).
 In addition to your base salary, you will receive an 8% holiday allowance and an 8.3% year-end bonus, both calculated based on your annual gross base salary.

Faculty of Humanities, Leiden University Centre for Linguistics 
 Is looking for: 
 Two PhD candidates, Descriptive/Documentary Linguistics in Indonesia
Starting date: Between February-July 2027; exact date to be determined by mutual agreement.
 Vacancy number: 16880 
 Deadline : October 25, 2026
 Description 
 Leiden University Centre for Linguistics (LUCL) invites applications for two fully funded PhD positions within the NWO project ‘Usku and Banda: Automated Documentation of Endangered Languages of Eastern Indonesia’.
 The two PhDs in this project will each work on the documentation and description of a small unwritten endangered language in eastern Indonesia.  
 The first PhD project focuses on Usku (also called Afra), a Papuan language spoken in the north-eastern part of the Indonesian province Papua in the western half of New Guinea. Usku is a moribund isolate with around 100 speakers that is surrounded by communities speaking languages belonging to other Papuan families. 
 The second PhD project focuses on Banda, an Austronesian language spoken by 4,000 speakers on the island of Kei Besar in the Indonesian province Maluku. 
 As the younger generations of speakers of Usku and Banda are reported to be switching to the dominant national language Indonesian, it is unlikely that the languages will be transmitted to the next generation, and both languages may become extinct within two generations. For this reason, documentation of these two unique languages is extremely urgent.
 For both Usku and Banda, the aim is to develop, in close collaboration with the speaker community, a documentary record of linguistic practices in the form of a rich, naturalistic text collection and an extensive word list (lexicon). The transcribed and annotated lexicon and corpus will form the basis of the grammatical analysis of the language’s phonology, morphology and syntax. This analysis will allow us to address questions such as: (i) How do the words and grammatical structures of Banda/Usku reflect possible inherited (vertical) family relationships and ancestral history? (ii) Which of these words and structures may have been acquired through (horizontal) contact with neighbouring languages or Indonesian/Malay? (iii) What does this tell us about the community’s socio-cultural history and their relationships with other communities? This information is expected to provide important insights into earlier patterns of migration and contact in the region.
 In the course of their documentation activities, both PhDs will test and evaluate the various AI tools that are being developed by the senior team members to carry out automated tasks of transcription, translation, morphological segmentation and glossing of data from small and underdocumented languages.  
 These PhD positions are part of an NWO-funded Open Competition Large project involving PI prof. dr. Marian Klamer, external partner dr. Eline Visser (Uppsala University) and research engineer dr. Sophie Villerius. 
 Tasks and responsibilities 
 Collecting audio-visual linguistic and cultural data through fieldwork in Indonesia; 
 Transcribing, annotating, analysing and archiving naturalistic language data; 
 Testing and evaluating tools for automated linguistic data annotation and analysis; 
 Presenting (joint) research results at workshops and conferences; 
 Publishing (joint) research results and writing a PhD-thesis within the period of appointment; 
 (Assisting in) teaching activities at bachelor level ; 
 (Assisting in) the organisation of knowledge dissemination activities 
 Participating in meetings and training sessions of the project research group 
 Selection criteria 
 A Master’s degree in linguistics, completed before the start date; 
 Demonstrated interest in language documentation, field linguistics, descriptive linguistics or similar; 
 Excellent research and academic English skills;   
 Working knowledge of Indonesian, or willingness to acquire this within the first half year of the project; 
 A strong cooperative attitude and interest to engage in collaborative research; 
 Fieldwork experience in a non-western context is a plus; 
 Preference will be given to candidates from Indonesia in cases of equal suitability. 
 Terms and conditions 
 Appointment will be according to the terms of the Collective Labour Agreement of Dutch Universities (CAO Nederlandse Universiteiten). The employment will be for a period of four years. The first contract will be for 12 months with an extension for the following 36 months contingent on a positive of performance and compatibility. You are expected to work in Leiden and the appointment must lead to the completion of a PhD thesis.
Salary range from € 3,204.- gross per month in the first year for a fulltime appointment to € 4,051.- in the fourth year (pay scale for PhDs, in accordance with the Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Universities), plus substantial additional holiday and year-end allowances. Candidates from outside the Netherlands may be eligible for a substantial tax break.
Starting date: Between February-July 2027; exact date to be determined by mutual agreement.
 Research at our faculty/ institute 
 Leiden University Centre for Linguistics ( LUCL ) is one of seven Institutes that falls under the Faculty of Humanities. With over 120 linguists working at the Institute, it is a rich research environment that prides itself on fostering scientific excellence. At LUCL we offer extensive research support to our researchers. 
 LUCL has a longstanding tradition in the study of the world’s languages and features unique linguistic expertise. Current theoretical insights are combined with modern methodological approaches in its research profile area ‘Language Diversity in the World’. Researchers from our  six umbrella research groups  are experts in their respective fields while finding innovative ways of collaborating with colleagues in other fields and disciplines.  
The Faculty of Humanities at Leiden University is a unique international centre for the advanced study of languages, cultures, arts, and societies worldwide, in their historical contexts from prehistory to the present.  Our faculty is home to more than 6,000 students and 800 staff members. For more information see: https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/humanities. 
 Diversity 
 Fostering an inclusive community is a central element of the values and vision of Leiden University. Leiden University is committed to becoming an inclusive community which enables all students and staff to feel valued and respected and to develop their full potential. Diversity in experiences and perspectives enriches our teaching and strengthens our research. High quality teaching and research is inclusive. 
 Questions? 
 For further information on the research project and the PhD positions please contact the PI, Marian Klamer, m.a.f.klamer@hum.leidenuniv.nl. 
 For practical questions, please contact the Institute Manager, Maarit van Gammeren: m.s.k.van.gammeren@hum.leidenuniv.nl . 
 Applications 
 Applications should be submitted no later than 25 October, 2026 via the blue button in our application system. Your application should include the following information:
 A cover letter, in which you indicate which of the two positions you are applying for  and explain your motivation;
 A full academic CV;
 A list of all Bachelor and Master-level modules you have taken, with an official transcript of grades;
 A writing sample, preferably your MA thesis and an article or term paper that you wrote that pertains to the topic of the position;
 The names and email addresses of two references, including your MA thesis supervisor(s), who may be approached by the selection committee (no reference letters).
 The vacancy closes on 25 October 2026. Interviews will take place in the first half of November 2026.
 Enquiries from agencies are not appreciated.

PhD Position on “Enhancing effective crisis decision-making at the strategic level” 
 The department of Social, Economic, and Organizational Psychology, Faculty of Social Sciences, Leiden University, invite applications for a 
 PhD Position in the context of the NWO Zwaartekracht consortium Adapt! (1 fte, 4 years) 
 The PhD candidate will be working within the NWO-funded Zwaartekracht consortium “Adapt!” and supervised by Prof. Dr. Daan Scheepers and Dr. Annabel Losecaat Vermeer (Social, Economic, and Organizational Psychology, Leiden University) and Prof. Dr. Arjen Boin (Political Science, Leiden University).
 The overall project 
The future of the open society depends on its adaptability to prepare for future crises. Adapt! investigates the role of cultural, social, and governmental capabilities of a society in building an effective and legitimate response to crises. Together with citizens and frontline professionals, the Adapt! consortium will translate research findings into tools and strategies that help societies navigate through crises. See https://adapt-academy.nl/en/ 
 The PhD position 
 In most large-scale crises—the Covid-19 pandemic being no exception—policy and organisational responses are shaped by high-level crisis decision-making groups such as executive boards, government cabinets, and senior coordination bodies. Despite their important role, relatively few empirical studies have examined the dynamics of, and decision-making within, these groups under crisis conditions. Strategic teams differ from operational teams in several important ways: their members are typically less trained and experienced with the task at hand and often lack detailed knowledge about the specific causes of—and possible responses to—the crisis.
 Using a series of group-based experiments, this PhD project examines group dynamics and decision-making in teams operating under crisis conditions characterized by uncertainty, novelty, incomplete information, time pressure, and high societal stakes. A particular focus is on leadership, including how leaders construe their power (as an opportunity versus a responsibility) and how accountability shapes team processes and decision-making.
 Key responsibilities 
 Develop and pilot a group decision-making paradigm and conduct a series of studies examining task process (e.g., information-sharing, advice taking) group dynamics (e.g., conflict, cohesion), and physiological indicators of stress and motivation.
 Collect, manage, and analyse behavioural and physiological data.
 Complete a PhD thesis in English within 4 years.
 Participate in regular meetings, and collaborative research activities within the research team, department, and Adapt! consortium.

This is achieved through collaboration, both within and outside the institute, in the field of psychology and related research areas, covering both fundamental and applied aspects. The broad bachelor’s program and a wide range of master’s specializations further contribute to this mission. Within the institute and the academic community, a dedicated and passionate atmosphere prevails. The themes of Health and Wellbeing, Social-Cognitive-Affective Decision Making, Development and Learning, and Advanced Behavioral Science Methods guide both research and education. The institute places great importance on fostering a safe and inclusive environment, with room for new developments such as open science, recognition and valorization, and interdisciplinarity, which are firmly embedded in the institute’s strategy. The institute, with approximately 5,000 students and 600 staff members, comprises the Institute Office, the Bachelor’s Education Department, and six research and teaching units: Health, Medical and Neuropsychology, Clinical Psychology, Cognitive Psychology, Developmental and Educational Psychology, Social and Organizational Psychology, and Methods and Statistics. What you bring

Are you an enthusiastic lawyer and/or public administration scholar with a curious research mind? Would you like to use your expertise to make a direct contribution to one of the major societal challenges of our time: the energy transition? Then we are looking for you!
 What are you going to do?
 As a PhD candidate, you will investigate how the regulation of the hydrogen economy can be designed in such a way that the law is better able to evolve alongside the economic sector and society that it seeks to regulate than is currently the case. The legal framework governing the energy transition often has a “static” character. It regulates what exists rather than what could exist. In a sector in which innovation is still developing rapidly, such as the hydrogen economy, a static legal framework can have a constraining effect on the development of the economy and society.
 An adaptive legal framework can prevent this problem, but it is not yet known what such a framework should entail or which adaptive instruments can effectively support the development of the hydrogen economy rather than constrain it.
 Within an ongoing research project, we are developing a theory of an adaptive legal framework for the hydrogen economy. In this project, we aim to empirically test this theoretical framework in order to determine which interpretation and application of the theory can be effective in practice. In this research, theory will be translated into verifiable hypotheses concerning governance and regulatory instruments for the hydrogen economy. These hypotheses will be tested both quantitatively, on the basis of experiments, and qualitatively, through semi-structured interviews.
 In developing this research, you will become part of an interdisciplinary research team within the HySuccess programme of GroenvermogenNL, in which you will work together with colleagues from different universities and disciplines.

Are you excited about developing new mathematical foundations for energy-efficient computing? Do you want to contribute to cutting-edge research at the intersection of systems and control theory, optimization, circuit theory, and neuromorphic computing?
 The University of Groningen is seeking a highly motivated PhD candidate to work on a fundamental research project on systems and control theory for learning in neuromorphic circuits. Neuromorphic computing is an analog, brain-inspired computing paradigm with the potential to drastically reduce energy consumption while enabling faster inference than conventional digital architectures. A major challenge, however, is the development and analysis of dedicated algorithms for training analog circuits directly from data.
 In this PhD project, you will develop a novel system-theoretic framework for learning in analog circuits and dissipative networks. We will view learning as a feedback interconnection of continuous-time (circuit) dynamics and an optimization algorithm. The key idea is to develop algorithms that minimise cost functions inspired by notions of energy, leading to highly efficient, local learning rules. 
 What are you going to do?
 As a PhD candidate, you will develop mathematical theory for learning in nonlinear and dynamic circuits. Building on preliminary results for resistive circuits, you will study circuits containing memristive and capacitive elements, as well as more general dissipative networks. The project combines systems and control theory, circuit theory, optimization, and machine learning, with the ultimate goal of advancing the mathematical foundations of physics-based learning.
 Your responsibilities include: 
 Developing a system-theoretic framework that models learning as the feedback interconnection between continuous-time circuit dynamics and optimization algorithms. 
 Designing novel energy-based learning algorithms for training analog circuits directly from input-output data.
 Developing fully decentralised learning rules that rely on local circuit information and are suitable for large-scale systems.
 Establishing rigorous theoretical guarantees for convergence and scalability of the proposed learning algorithms.
 Extending the theory from analog circuits to more general dissipative networks.
 Testing and validating the developed methods.
 Publishing research findings in leading international journals and conferences and presenting your work at scientific meetings.
 Contributing to teaching activities and supervising Bachelor's and Master's students where appropriate.

How to best incorporate New Genomic Techniques to solve challenging issues in plant breeding? The recent approval by the European Parliament of new legislation to allow application of gene editing approaches in plant breeding, offers new opportunities to address this. One such challenge is to improve complex traits such as crop tolerance to dynamic environmental conditions in the current era of global climate change and how to best incorporate this in plant breeding strategies.
Anticipating the new legislation, the INPROBED project has been granted, which aims to precisely identify and modify cis -regulatory elements and transcription factor genes that control key physiological pathways to specifically adjust targeted gene expression to reshape complex traits.
The project will develop a breakthrough science-enabled technology platform to improve tomato heat, drought and nutrient deficiency tolerance and the nutritional status of tomato fruits for human health. In this project, you will investigate the tomato response to Zn and Fe deficiency and design strategies to improve the Zn/Fe nutritional status of tomatoes for human health.
You will generate dedicated (single-cell) transcriptional data sets feeding into the MNase-defined cistrome occupancy (MOA-seq) analysis of transcription factor binding of tomato promoter elements controlling the Zn and Fe deficiency responsive gene expression. You will design specific constructs to edit transcription factor genes and their target promoters, and analyse the effects of optimized gene expression regulation on plant performance under optimal and field-like conditions at the Netherlands Plant Eco-phenotyping Centre. Your research aims to improve tomato Zn and Fe uptake under regular field conditions and to enhance the Zn and Fe nutritional status of tomato fruits.
INPROBED is part of the prestigious European Innovation Council (EIC) Pathfinder Challenge programme addressing innovative biotechnology for climate resilient crops. It brings together excellent expertise from world-leading European research institutions and companies. You will work closely together with researchers across the consortium to predict and edit targeted gene promoters, to design relevant constructs for gene editing and to evaluate the gene-edited plants to establish this topic firmly into the plant breeding domain.
Within Wageningen University, you will be embedded in the Laboratory of Genetics of the Plant Sciences Group, and collaborate with researchers and thesis students investigating the genetic basis of plant adaptation to the environment, focusing on plant nutrition, metal tolerance and photosynthesis. Your research is expected to deliver fundamental insights into the genetic regulation of tomato gene expression and provide strong experimental validation of the technology platform to improve complex crop traits through gene editing of gene expression regulators.
 Your duties and responsibilities include: 
 To design the experimental setup for gene expression analysis of tomato response to Zn and Fe deficiency, and of Zn and Fe loading into the developing fruit.
 The biological interpretation of MOA-seq analysis with respect to the tomato response to Zn and Fe deficiency.
 The experimental validation of gene-edited tomato plants with respect to plant growth and development and their ionome under optimal, natural and mineral-stress conditions.
 To establish a fruitful collaboration with international partners in the project and to supervise a part-time technician on the project.
 To write manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed scientific journals reporting on the results of your research.
 Your team 
You will work with international partners in the project and with other members in the Botanical Genetics team of the Laboratory of Genetics of Wageningen University, which is led by Prof. Mark Aarts You will work in close collaboration with a technician to be appointed on the project.
 You will work here 
Wageningen UR has a global reputation for its ground-breaking research and innovative education in the fields of food and health, sustainable agrosystems, the rural environment, and societal development - all of which make an essential contribution to the quality of life, i.e. the supply of safe and healthy food and drink, on the one hand, and the chance to live, work and play in a balanced ecosystem with a large variety of plants and animals on the other. Within Wageningen UR, the Plant Sciences Group brings together science education and scientific, strategic and applied research in the fields of biology, of plants in relation to their environment, of plant-related organisms and of plant production. The Laboratory of Genetics is interested in heredity in general, in particular the origin, architecture and consequences of genetic variation of a wide range of organisms across the biological kingdoms.

REQUIREMENTS:
You are an ambitious, curiosity-driven and collaboration-oriented plant scientist, with:
 a strong academic track record and a PhD in plant biotechnology, plant molecular genetics or a related topic;
 experience with plant mineral homeostasis and/or tomato research;
 demonstrated expertise in the analysis of large data-sets;
 a strong interest in experimental research;
 an excellent oral and written English communication skills.
In our international working environment there is an increasing amount of communication in English. For this position it is about language level C1 .

Do you want to contribute to the scientific and engineering foundations of the next generation of sustainable structural steels? 
 Job description 
The steel industry is undergoing a major transformation to reduce its environmental impact. New production routes based on hydrogen direct reduced iron (DRI), electric arc furnaces (EAF), and the increased use of scrap are expected to play a key role in the decarbonization of the steel sector. However, important questions remain regarding the performance of these next-generation sustainable steels in fatigue-critical infrastructure and structural applications.
In this PhD project, you will investigate the fatigue performance and weldability of next-generation structural steels, with the aim of enabling their safe application in infrastructure and construction. Specifically, the research will examine how "greener" steel production routes and varying levels of scrap content affect the fatigue behaviour and the weldability of these sustainable structural steels. You will combine experimental testing with advanced numerical modelling to evaluate both the base material and welded joints. The project will also assess whether existing fatigue design methods developed for conventional steels remain applicable to these next-generation sustainable steels.
As a PhD candidate, you will be part of the Grow with Green Steel ( Groeien met Groen Staal ) programme and work within a multidisciplinary consortium of leading universities, research institutes, and industrial partners. This unique collaboration offers an excellent opportunity to contribute to cutting-edge research while working closely with stakeholders across the steel value chain. The outcomes of the project will support the safe implementation of the next-generation structural steels in fatigue-critical infrastructure and structural applications. Furthermore, the research will help reduce technical uncertainties associated with the transition towards a more sustainable and circular steel industry.
The Steel & Composites section at TU Delft conducts research on the behaviour, design, and assessment of steel and composite structures under both static and fatigue loading. Its research is built on a strong combination of experimental and numerical approaches, ranging from material characterization and component testing to full-scale structural demonstrators supported by advanced modelling techniques. The section is well positioned to address challenges related to sustainable and resilient infrastructure, contributing to the transition towards a circular and climate-neutral built environment.
 Job requirements 
 You hold an MSc degree in Civil/Structural Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Materials Science, or a related field.
 You have a background in structural performance of steel. Additonal knowledge of its fatigue and welding behaviour is an advantage.
 You enjoy combining experimental work in a structural lab environmnent, with numerical and analytical approaches.
 You communicate effectively in English and enjoy collaborating with academic and industrial partners.
 You are comfortable working in a multidisciplinary and international environment.
 TU Delft (Delft University of Technology) 
Working at TU Delft means contributing to solutions that really make a difference.
For over 180 years, we have been training engineers who make an impact worldwide in companies, government bodies, or as entrepreneurs. Our alumni turn knowledge into concrete solutions for the challenges of today and tomorrow. These challenges are changing rapidly. That is why we focus on themes such as energy, climate, digitalisation, artificial intelligence (AI), and smart mobility every day. Our education and research are directly aligned with what society needs now and in the future.
At TU Delft, our people make the difference. With their knowledge and curiosity, our staff provide a high-quality education and conduct pioneering research that extends beyond the campus. You will have the opportunity to take the initiative, work with others, and grow as a professional. Working at TU Delft means join an international community of professionals and students. Together, we create knowledge, innovations, and solutions that help move the world forward.
 Faculty of Civil Engineering and Geosciences 
The Faculty of Civil Engineering & Geosciences (CEG) is committed to outstanding international research and education in the field of civil engineering, applied earth sciences, traffic and transport, water technology, and delta technology. Our research feeds into our educational programmes and covers societal challenges such as climate change, energy transition, resource availability, urbanisation and clean water. Our research projects are conducted in close cooperation with a wide range of research institutions. The Faculty of Economics and Business offers an inspiring study and working environment for students and employees. International accreditation enables the Faculty to assess performance against the highest international standards. It also creates an exciting environment of continuous improvement. FEB's programs, academic staff, and research do well on various excellence ranking lists.
 The Faculty of Economics and Business has one PhD position available in the field of Organizational Behavior. The position is embedded in FEBRI, the Faculty’s research institute.
 What are you going to do?
 The PhD project is part of a recently awarded NWO SSH Open Competition L grant to the supervisors Prof. Floor Rink, Prof. Janka Stoker, and Prof. Michelle Ryan, entitled “ Beyond access: A career trajectory perspective on gender equality at the top ” (NWO 406.L.25EB.013). Women’s representation in senior leadership is increasing, yet gender inequality at the top persists. This PhD project moves beyond the question of how women gain access to senior positions and examines what happens next. You will study whether women and men follow different career trajectories after their first senior leadership appointment, with particular attention to exits from leadership and subsequent moves into new roles. The project asks whether, and when, apparently voluntary exits may reflect pressure or constrained choice; whether such exit experiences differ by gender; and whether leaders’ next appointments represent upward, lateral, or downward leadership moves. The project further aims to identify conditions that stabilize (or destabilize) men’s and women’s leadership careers over time. You will develop the studies in close collaboration with the supervisory team. To study the research questions, we will collect and integrate media data on the exits and reappointments of executive leaders with longitudinal quantitative career data. The aim is to produce a PhD dissertation that advances theory on gendered patterns in leadership while generating evidence relevant to organizations and policymakers.

euraxess:465745.description:
Are you fascinated by how curiosity shapes learning in the classroom? Would you like to investigate how children seek information, explore and learn in real-world educational settings? If so, then we invite you to apply for this PhD position on Curiosity in the Classroom at Radboud University.
Curiosity is a powerful driver of learning, yet we still know relatively little about how curiosity unfolds in the classroom and how educational environments can support children in becoming curious and actively seeking information. In this PhD project, you will investigate curiosity in 10-to 12-year-old children within authentic educational settings.
The project combines experimental research, classroom studies and computational modelling to better understand what makes children curious, how they decide which information to explore, and how different ways of structuring learning environments influence curiosity and learning. Computational models will be used to characterise individual differences in information-seeking behaviour and to examine how these differences relate to learning in the classroom. A central aim is to translate insights from fundamental research on curiosity into educational practice.
You will design and conduct studies in collaboration with primary schools and educational partners, review the scientific literature, recruit and test participants, develop and evaluate educational materials and experimental tasks, analyse behavioural data, apply computational modelling techniques, and write scientific articles that will form the basis of your dissertation.
You will work closely with your supervisors, another PhD candidate investigating the cognitive neuroscience of curiosity, and a broader interdisciplinary team of researchers in psychology, cognitive neuroscience and educational science. You will also collaborate with schools, teachers and educational organisations to conduct research in real-world learning environments.
The position involves frequent communication with children, parents, teachers, schools and other stakeholders, presenting your work to national and international audiences, and contributing to teaching for approximately 10% of your time.
 Would you like to learn more about what it’s like to pursue a PhD at Radboud University? Visit the page about working as a PhD candidate .

ADDITIONAL INFORMATION:
Benefits We will give you a temporary employment contract (1.0 FTE) of 1.5 years, after which your performance will be evaluated. If the evaluation is positive, your contract will be extended by 2.5 years (4-year contract).
 You will receive a starting salary of €3,204 gross per month based on a 38-hour working week, which will increase to €4,051 in the fourth year ( salary scale P ).
 You will receive an 8% holiday allowance and an 8,3% end-of-year bonus.
 You will receive extra days off. With full-time employment, you can choose between 30 or 41 days of annual leave instead of the statutory 20.
 Additional employment conditions 
Work and science require good employment practices. This is reflected in Radboud University's primary and secondary employment conditions . You can make arrangements for the best possible work-life balance with flexible working hours, various leave arrangements and working from home. You are also able to compose part of your employment conditions yourself, for example, exchange income for extra leave days and receive a reimbursement for your sports subscription. And of course, we offer a good pension plan. You are given plenty of room and responsibility to develop your talents and realise your ambitions. Therefore, we provide various training and development schemes.

PhD position on local food web dynamics within offshore wind farms in the North Sea POWER (Progress in Offshore Wind Ecological Research) consortium. 
As offshore wind farms rapidly expand in the North Sea, mitigating their ecological impact on marine ecosystems is critical. The North Sea POWER project addresses this challenge by filling vital knowledge gaps regarding underwater noise, biomass and water flows, and wildlife disturbance (such as seabirds and bats) to support a sustainable green energy transition. By reducing uncertainty in models and identifying effective mitigation options, North Sea POWER supports offshore wind development that protects marine ecosystems while contributing to a sustainable energy future.
The project is funded through the Dutch Research Agenda (NWA), developed in collaboration with the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy.
Led by Wageningen University & Research, the project brings together a transdisciplinary consortium of leading academic institutions, societal stakeholders, conservation organisations, and energy sector partners. More about the consortium .
This position is one of twelve PhD and postdoc positions across the consortium. You will be part of a team working on shared questions, with joint meetings, fieldwork and training alongside your own project. You will be hosted at Wageningen Marine Research in Den Helder, where you will study how fouling communities in offshore wind farms affect local food web dynamics and carbon cycling in close collaboration with Wageningen University. Part of the molecular lab work will be performed in the lab of Marine Animal Ecology in Wageningen.
 Are you interested in how biofouling communities in offshore wind farms affect local food web dynamics and carbon cycling? 
We are looking for a motivated PhD candidate to join our research team on biofouling with a focus on quantifying how biofouling communities influence primary and secondary production and blue carbon sequestration in the seabed. By combining laboratory experiments, in-situ fieldwork observations, and ecosystem modelling, your work will help refine current ecosystem-scale models and inform environmental impact assessments.
 Your duties and responsibilities include: 
 conduct laboratory experiments to measure and quantify grazing rates, carbon biomass, prey preferences, particle export, and faeces sinking velocity rates across different fouling species;
 execute field surveys from research vessels;
 integrate empirical data into conceptual models;
 publish research findings in peer-reviewed journals and present them at national and international conferences;
 mentor BSc/MSc students.
 Your team 
You will be part of Wageningen Marine Research (WMR – Den Helder), as a member of the Theme Team North Sea Reefs with Dr. Joop Coolen , and Dr. Ninon Mavraki as your daily supervisors, and you are also part of the Marine Animal Ecology Group (MAE) supervised by the Associate Professor Reindert Nijland at Wageningen University and Research. In Den Helder a broad group of scientists, analysts, field workers and students work on a variety of topics, such as benthic ecology, seals, seabirds, bats and other species. You will be a member of the theme team North Sea Reefs, with multiple colleagues specialising in the ecology of natural and artificial reefs in the North Sea. Furthermore, you will have the opportunity to design experiments involving molecular tools, such as eDNA and DNA metabarcoding, which then will be performed at the molecular laboratory of MAE in Wageningen University.
 You will work here 
The position is available within Wageningen University & Research at the Marine Animal Ecology group. The organisation has good and flexible employment conditions, including good education and training facilities for PhD students. Your working location will be at Wageningen Marine Research in Den Helder, the Netherlands, where the daily supervisors Joop Coolen and Ninon Mavraki are located. WMR is an applied research institute with 3 locations (Den Helder, IJmuiden and Yerseke) in the Netherlands. Research areas in Den Helder include coastal and offshore North Sea, tropics and (ant)arctic regions. In addition to ecological research, WMR advises the government regarding protection of species and habitats, pollution, and other anthropogenic interactions with ecology, and collaborate with industry, i.a. to study nature inclusive designs. Facilities in Den Helder in addition to offices, include a benthic lab, eco-analysis lab, climate rooms, mesocosms and algae culture facilities. Additionally, WMR has an experimental hard substrate garden in the marina on the island of Texel.

REQUIREMENTS:
You are/have the following: 
 you have a master’s degree (or graduation before appointment date) in Biology, Marine Biology, Ecology, Environmental Science, or another closely related field;
 you have experience with hands-on laboratory experiments and ecological fieldwork;
 you have demonstrated background or strong interest in ecological modelling and data analysis;
 you have a strong interest in marine ecology and multidisciplinary research;
 you also have strong collaborative skills and are willing to work with a diverse group of scientists, technicians, and project stakeholders with various backgrounds.
Furthermore, you have strong quantitative and preferably technical skills, and the ability to work independently in a challenging environment.
 You also possess: 
you have a proactive, inquisitive, enthusiastic, creative and self-reliant mind-set and you are strongly motivated to obtain a PhD degree.
Finally, you are excellent in written and oral communication skills in English (a minimum of CEFR C2 level language proficiency). For more information about this proficiency level, please visit our special language page .

CONTRACT: 18 months

 Information 
We are looking for a highly motivated PhD candidate with a background in photonics, optics, or nanofabrication to contribute to SPARK Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral network. The candidate will develop chip-scale metamaterials with time-varying modulation for nonreciprocal photonic devices. The project involves theoretical and numerical design of dynamically modulated structures, on-chip fabrication using advanced nanolithography, and experimental demonstration of nonreciprocal light transport, with the aim of realizing dynamically modulated metamaterials for nonreciprocal light control and integrating them into photonic circuits for optical communication and quantum applications.
The PhD candidate will work within the Photonic Integration group at the Department of Electrical Engineering, Eindhoven University of Technology, co-supervised by Prof. M. Piccardo at INESC MN, Portugal. The candidate will be part of a multidisciplinary, international team within the SPARK MSCA Doctoral network, working alongside PhD students and researchers on related nonreciprocal and photonic integration technologies, with close collaboration across design, fabrication, and characterization.
The research and secondment activities will be supported by a 6-month stay at INESC MN, Portugal, focused on component measurements, and a 3-month stay at PICadvanced for chip-level integration, giving the candidate direct access to complementary expertise and facilities across the consortium.

The Department of Coastal Systems (COS) at the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research (NIOZ-Texel) is looking for a highly motivated early career postdoctoral researcher to help develop a pilot-scale seagrass nursery that will support long-term, large-scale ecosystem restoration. We are looking for an experimental scientist with a background in aquatic or marine plant physiology, ecophysiology, biogeochemistry, or a related field, who is excited to apply fundamental knowledge of plant functioning to a major challenge in coastal ecosystem restoration. 
 THE DEPARTMENT 
 The Department of COS studies integral coastal ecosystems and their populations of fish, birds, and other marine animals in the North and Wadden Seas as well as on a global scale. The department focusses on key physical, chemical and biological processes that determine the productivity and the ecological functioning of coastal areas. The coastal system is studied as a unity by considering the interrelations between the key compartments of the ecosystem (water, sediment, microalgae, macrozoobenthos, parasites, fish and birds). The welcoming atmosphere at NIOZ will provide ample opportunity for collaborations.
 THE PROJECT 
 Seagrass meadows are important coastal ecosystems but have largely disappeared from the Dutch Wadden Sea. Active restoration is now producing promising results, yet further upscaling is constrained by the availability of seeds and plants from natural donor populations. To overcome this bottleneck, NIOZ and partners are developing a pilot-scale seagrass nursery in Lauwersoog.
 Building on successful cultivation experiments and pilot trials, the project will develop a 160-m² nursery producing seeds and plants of Zostera marina and Nanozostera noltei for restoration in the Wadden Sea. A key challenge is to optimize the biological cultivation process by understanding and controlling the environmental conditions that determine plant growth and reproduction. The project thereby connects fundamental plant ecophysiology and biogeochemistry directly to large-scale ecosystem restoration.
 THE POSITION 
 You will take a leading scientific role in developing and optimizing seagrass cultivation in the pilot nursery. Through experiments ranging from aquaria to large outdoor cultivation units, you will unravel how nutrient availability, inorganic carbon, light and environmental cues affect seagrass growth and reproduction, and how these factors can be manipulated to optimize cultivation.
 In your work, you will combine hypothesis-driven experimental research with hands-on development and optimization of a new seagrass cultivation system. You will work closely with NIOZ researchers, technical staff and external project partners, and translate your findings into practical cultivation protocols for producing seagrass restoration material at scale.

REQUIREMENTS:
THE CANDIDATE 
 You hold a PhD in a relevant discipline, such as plant physiology, plant ecophysiology, aquatic plant biology, marine botany, biogeochemistry or aquatic ecology, and have experience with hypothesis-driven experimental research. We particularly encourage applications from researchers with a strong background in plant physiology or biogeochemistry who are interested in applying their expertise to marine ecology and ecosystem restoration. Previous experience with seagrasses is an advantage but is not essential. 
 You enjoy combining rigorous experimental science with practical problem solving and are comfortable working hands-on with living plants, cultivation systems and monitoring equipment. You are able to analyse and interpret experimental data, communicate your findings clearly in English, and enjoy collaborating across disciplinary and organisational boundaries. An affinity with ecology and ecosystem restoration is essential.
 NIOZ is committed to a healthy and an inclusive working environment, in which people from diverse backgrounds can contribute and develop their talents. We value transparent and inclusive decision-making and expect our leaders to demonstrate visible commitment to inclusion, awareness of bias, and cultural intelligence.
 THE CONDITIONS 
 Employment of this position for 40 hours a week at Royal NIOZ NWO-I for a duration of 3 years.
 Salary compliant with CAO-WVOI (Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Research Institutes) scale 10 depending on relevant experience.
 The freedom to fulfill your role and space and opportunities for your personal (talent) development with the help of the NIOZ Academy.
 338 annualized holiday hours for a full-time 40-hour work week.

PhD position on bio-optics, in the North Sea POWER (Progress in Offshore Wind Ecological Research) consortium 
 The Department of Estuarine & Delta Systems (EDS) - location Yerseke of NIOZ is looking for a highly motivated and proactive PhD candidate to investigate the underwater light climate around offshore wind farms in the North Sea. 
 ROYAL NIOZ 
 NWO-NIOZ Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research is the Dutch national oceanographic institute and principally performs academically excellent multidisciplinary, fundamental, and frontier applied marine research addressing important scientific and societal questions pertinent to the functioning of the ocean and seas. NIOZ includes the National Marine research Facilities (NMF) department that operates a fleet of research vessels and the national pool of large seagoing equipment, and supports excellence in multidisciplinary marine research, education, and policy development.
 THE PROJECT 
 As offshore wind farms rapidly expand in the North Sea, mitigating their ecological impact on marine ecosystems is critical. The North Sea POWER project addresses this challenge by filling vital knowledge gaps regarding underwater noise, biomass and water flows, and wildlife disturbance (such as seabirds and bats) to support a sustainable green energy transition. By reducing uncertainty in models and identifying effective mitigation options, North Sea POWER supports offshore wind development that protects marine ecosystems while contributing to a sustainable energy future. The project is funded through the Dutch Research Agenda (NWA), developed in collaboration with the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy. Led by Wageningen University & Research, the project brings together a transdisciplinary consortium of leading academic institutions, societal stakeholders, conservation organisations, and energy sector partners. More about the consortium
 This position is one of twelve PhD and postdoc positions across the consortium. You will be part of a team working on shared questions, with joint meetings, fieldwork and training alongside your own project. You will be hosted at NIOZ in Yerseke, where you will study bio-optics in close collaboration with NIOZ on Texel, Deltares as well as University of Twente.
 THE POSITION 
 Do you want to unravel how offshore wind farms (OWF’s) are transforming the underwater light environment of the North Sea? To reveal this, you will develop inversion algorithms to derive the underwater light climate and other optical water quality parameters from satellite data of the North Sea. In this PhD position, you will measure spectra, light scattering, absorption and attenuation, and concentrations of optically active substances during North Sea ship cruises and in the laboratory. Using radiative transfer and optical modelling techniques, you will develop inversion algorithms that will quantify changes in the in-water light field and biogeochemical variables. By comparing ecosystem model simulations with and without offshore wind farms against the satellite-derived observations and in-situ data, you will assess the impact of these OWFs. Your work will also support formulation of light processes in ecosystem models for understanding the ecological effects of the OWFs.

About DETECTIVE 
 DETECTIVE (Data driven Excellence in Training of Epidemiological, Clinical, Technological and Innovative Virus Experts) is an EU-funded MSCA training programme aimed at developing new, data-driven methods to anticipate, detect and respond to emerging viral threats at an earlier stage than before. Coordinated by Prof. Dr. Heli Harvala, Professor of Virology at the University of Turku in Finland, the network brings together 8 academic institutions and 14 associated partners from across Europe. 
 Within DETECTIVE, researchers will develop innovative methods used to detect emerging pathogens earlier, understand who is most at risk, and translate the complex multi-source data into real-time, evidence-based decisions and clinical applications. The project's overall goal is to establish a unified, end-to-end epidemic-intelligence frame work, enhancing Europe’s capacity to respond to threats quickly and in a coordinated manner. This will be achieved by an integrated approach combining virology, evolutionary genomics, epidemiology, diagnostics and AI-based analytical methods. 
 Background of Project DC4 
 Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases represent one of the greatest threats to global health and societal stability in the 21st century. This PhD position focuses on developing and implementing an automated, AI‑assisted virus culture and characterisation platform. You will integrate next‑generation sequencing (NGS), serology and image‑based AI with practical virological diagnostics to enable faster, smarter detection and characterisation of emerging viral pathogens. Enteroviruses, with their diverse culture characteristics, will be an ideal training ground to develop methods that can later be applied to other emerging viruses. 
 You will work on several aspects ranging  from high‑throughput isolation of outbreak strains using AI, to mapping antigenic divergence for epidemic risk assessment, and generating fully characterised virus panels to support diagnostic and surveillance laboratories across Europe. In addition, you will consider ethical and practical aspects of data sharing and biobanking in the context of epidemic preparedness. 
 You will join the PhD program at the Graduate School of Life Sciences   
 https://www.uu.nl/en/education/graduate-school-of-life-sciences .  
 Job Description  
 For the innovative DETECTIVE project (“Data driven Excellence in Training of Epidemiological, Clinical, Technological and Innovative Virus Experts”), we are looking for an enthusiastic PhD candidate who is motivated to obtain a doctorate that combines cutting‑edge virological laboratory techniques with bioinformatics and AI‑based data analysis. 
 During this four‑year PhD trajectory you will: 
 Develop and optimise automated, AI‑based virus culture workflows, including image‑analysis algorithms to detect cytopathic effects earlier and more consistently than traditional read‑outs for a broad range of viruses, using enteroviruses as a model system. 
 Perform laboratory experiments, including sample handling, cell culture, virus isolation, nucleic‑acid extraction and NGS library preparation. 
 Integrate sequencing and serological data to link genotype, phenotype and antigenic characteristics of virus isolates, including risk analyses for clinical and public‑health purposes. 
 Linking culture‑based detection to functional assays (in collaboration other DCs in DETECTIVE) to validate phenotypic findings in organoid platforms and explore implications for vaccine and antiviral research. 
 Establish and refine reduced‑serum (low‑FBS) culture strategies to improve standardisation and sustainability of virus isolation. 
 Contribute to building and maintaining a central biobank of fully characterised virus isolates and associated metadata for future diagnostic and research use. 
 Collaborate with colleagues on quality‑control panels and harmonized laboratory protocols regarding isolation, serology and sequencing for European surveillance laboratories within the DETECTIVE network. 
 Analyse and interpret complex datasets of the integrated workflow (culture, NGS and serology) with bioinformatics and data‑science tools, in close collaboration with the DETECTIVE DCs and partners and with national and international partners. 
 Publish your results in scientific journals, present at (inter)national conferences, and translate your findings into practical recommendations for diagnostics and public health. 
 Alongside scientific expertise, you will develop personal and professional skills through training modules within the doctoral programme, for example in project and time management, scientific communication and advanced data analysis. The skills you acquire during this PhD will provide a strong foundation for a career in research, healthcare or public health. 
 The PhD will be hosted at the National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) in the Netherlands. You will be enrolled as a PhD candidate at U

Are you our next PhD candidate in functional data analysis? Are you passionate about developing statistical methodology for complex, dynamic data? Join our team to develop methods for estimating time-varying network structures and detecting structural changes in functional time series.
 Information 
In many scientific fields, observations are increasingly collected in the form of functions rather than simple numerical measurements. Examples include brain signals recorded continuously over time, and economic indicators observed as curves or distributions. Such functional time series often exhibit temporal dependence, non-stationarity, and complex non-Euclidean structures. These features contain valuable information, but they also make conventional statistical methods difficult to apply and can lead to unreliable conclusions.
Network structures provide a useful way to describe the relationships among the components of these complex data. In neuroscience, for example, connections between brain regions may be inferred from functional imaging signals rather than observed directly. Understanding which connections are present, how they evolve over time, and when structural changes occur is essential for scientific interpretation. Existing methods may produce false or missed connections when the observations are dependent, non-stationary, and non-Euclidean.
In this project, you will investigate theoretical tools for analysing dependence structures in functional time series. You will develop new methods and statistical softwares for constructing time-varying networks, detecting structural changes, and controlling false connections in complex settings. The proposed methods will contribute to deeper insights in distinguishing connections and changes from random variation in scientific studies. The PhD candidate will be supervised by Lujia Bai and Jeanine Duistermaat , and will publish in international scientific journals, participate in international conferences, and develop an independent research profile.
You will join the Statistics, Probability and Operations Research (SPOR) cluster in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at Eindhoven University of Technology. The cluster offers a collaborative research environment that connects time series analysis, functional data and network analysis. We work closely with external partners who drive innovation and growth, and our research is strongly embedded in applications such as anomaly detection, process monitoring and improvement, weather and climate forecasting, and statistical bioinformatics.
As an ideal candidate, you have a strong affinity for mathematical statistics and rigorous proofs, as well as a passion for developing and implementing novel methods and applying them to real-world data.

REQUIREMENTS:
A master’s degree in Statistics, Mathematics, Econometrics or related majors.
 Motivated to develop your teaching skills and coach students.
 Fluent in spoken and written English (C1 level).
 Good programming skills preferably in R or Python. Experience in programming with C++.
 Prior knowledge in time series analysis, functional data analysis or functional analysis is of benefit .
 Excellent communication skills.

CONTRACT: 4 years

Within the MEDAL project (Motivating mEaningful Daily Data collection through Design, AI, and SociaL engagement, https://www.clicknl.nl/en/ontwerpkrachtentransities/medal/ ), TU/e leads a consortium — including Catharina Hospital, Fashion Tech Farm, and other creative and knowledge partners like Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences — investigating how personal life data, alongside clinical measurements, can find a place in cardiovascular care pathways. The recurring tension here: patients at home need data that is both clinically usable and effortless to fit into daily life. This EngD track works out that tension specifically for the heart failure care pathway.
 Assignment 
You research and design how contextual data - living patterns, activity, emotional and social signals - can be used alongside physiological measurements to support heart failure patients in self-management at home.
 Co-design workshops with heart failure patients and healthcare professionals at Catharina Hospital to identify data needs and interaction preferences. You can work with the team in the hospital who already redesigned and develop the care pathway.
 Translate these insights into design requirements for data collection, visualization, and feedback.
 Collaborate with Fashion Tech Farm on a tangible, textile-based exploration of what this health data can feel like — a more explorative, conceptual counterpart to the functional prototype, probing wearable and material forms of data experience beyond screens and numbers.
 Develop and iterate a data-driven prototype for home monitoring, working with technology partners like Cardiron.
 Run real-world pilot tests on subjects like usability, clinical relevance, user engagement, and impact on home-based self-management.
 Outcome 
A validated prototype, embedded in the existing systems in the hospital for participatory home care for heart failure patients, alongside a textile/tangible design exploration developed with Fashion Tech Farm that opens up alternative, more embodied forms of engaging with health data. Together these feed the design principles contributed to the broader MEDAL framework for data interaction in participatory healthcare.

Are you fascinated by controlling magnetic matter by femtosecond laser pulses, eager to explore the underlying physical mechanisms, and passionate to develop a generic tool to ‘print’ complex textures just by design? Join us as a PhD candidate on the ERC project “Topological Magnetism by Photonic Design” – TOP DESIGN!
 Information 
Topology is a fundamental concept with intriguing implications. Central in your project will be the skyrmion – a nanoscale, whirling magnetic texture. Skyrmions are topologically protected and act like particles; they can be created, moved and annihilated – ideal to store and carry information. Imagine being able to create and delete skyrmions on demand at any position. Imagine doing so for more complex textures, or, ultimately, creating synthetic lattices of skyrmionic entities just by design. That’s the challenge you will address, to open up new horizons in fundamental research, but also to enable non-conventional, more sustainable ICT solutions.
Within the overarching ERC Advanced Grant project “Topological Magnetism by Photonic Design” (TOP DESIGN) two PhD candidates will do their fundamental experimental physics research in a larger team, supervised by Prof. Bert Koopmans, based at Eindhoven University of Technology.
PhD candidate 1 will explore fundamental processes underlying the deterministic creation and annihilation of sub-diffraction limited skyrmions by sequences of femtosecond laser pulses, using a suite of femtosecond time-resolved magneto-optical spectroscopies, as well as magnetic imaging using a dedicated magnetic force microscope and magnetic electron microscopy. PhD candidate 2 will use this fundamental understanding to extrapolate towards more complex textures, including entire lattices and guided by state-of-the-art nano-lithographies, in order to develop a versatile ‘magnetic topology printer’. Both PhD candidates will design and synthesize multilayered magnetic thin films using the NanoAccess facility, and will enjoy theoretical support by a more experienced theoretical postdoc. In the second phase of the project, work will move towards current-driven dynamics of the nanosized textures, the exploration of topological excitations, and final steps towards implementation in an integrated photonic platform, for which an additional PhD candidate and postdoc will join the team.
Within the team you will closely collaborate, but you will also profit from a strong international network. You will publish your findings in research articles in leading journals and by giving talks and presenting posters at national and international research conferences. During the four-year period of the PhD position, you will grow into an independent researcher who can conduct research in a collaborative environment. Moreover, you will improve your teaching and supervision skills by the 10% teaching and supervisions tasks scheduled within your employment.

Job description 
QuTech, the research center of Delft University of Technology (TU Delft) is hiring for a Doctoral Candidate (PhD) position in partnership with the Questing Doctoral Network.
The QUESTING Doctoral Network is a European doctoral training initiative funded by the Horizon Europe Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA). The Doctoral Network’s aim is to address the major skills shortage in quantum technology by training researchers who will help build the future of secure and efficient communication networks: the Quantum Internet.
 PhD project - Important the start date for this PhD is 1 st December 2026. 
 PhD Position Topic: Enhancing Entanglement Quality in Quantum Networks
We welcome applications for this Doctoral position whose goal is to expand, improve and evaluate our existing set of tools for improving the quality of entanglement between network nodes. Potential directions are improving techniques for entanglement distillation, potentially through a connection with error correction, and the use of discarding low-quality entanglement (cut-off time). We will use simulation and analytical calculation for doing so.
As part of the Doctoral Network collaboration his position includes research stays of few months at:
 University of Naples Federico II (UNINA), Italy.
 EURECOM, France.
In addition to these secondments, the position offers interdisciplinary training within the Doctoral Network.
 Research groups 
This project will be conducted within Tim Coopmans’ research group at QuTech, the quantum research institute of Delft University of Technology. The group focuses on the design of quantum networks and quantum circuits using techniques from (formal) computer science.
You will work closely with this growing team, where most members, including the first PhD candidates who joined in September last year, are at a similar stage of their research journey. The current group has a mixed BSc/MSc background, ranging from computer science to physics, electrical engineering and mathematics.
Here at QuTech, we are committed to fostering an inclusive and diverse research environment, and we strongly encourage applications from women and candidates from underrepresented groups, including but not limited to those from diverse cultural, socioeconomic, and educational backgrounds.
This commitment is reflected within the group as well: Tim Coopmans is a mentor in the WIQD mentorship programme (WIQD: "We In Quantum Development", formerly "Women In Quantum Development", https://www.wiqd.nl/ ).
 Job requirements 
We are looking for a motivated and creative researcher interested in working at the intersection of quantum technology, quantum information, and computer science. Challenge: Accelerate the transition towards circular and resilient buildings. 
 Change: Develop multi-scale assessment methods. 
 Impact: Enable scalable pathways for urban environments. 
 Job description 
The Faculty of Architecture and the Built Environment of Delft University of Technology is hiring a PhD researcher to work on a recently awarded Horizon Europe project, entitled AURORA (Shaping safe, sustainable, and human-centered places) under the supervision of Assistant Professors Simona Bianchi and Olga Ioannou, and Associate Professor Maria Pregnolato.
The broader AURORA project aims at accelerating the transformation of the built environment towards climate resilience and circularity. The project has a strong social perspective aiming at both technological and governance innovation. It combines innovative construction technologies, digital workflows, multi-level governance approaches, and participatory processes to support the development and implementation of resilient renovation strategies. Through demonstration pilots across Europe, AURORA provides practical frameworks for municipalities, practitioners, and stakeholders to evaluate and implement sustainable construction and renovation pathways.
In your role as a PhD researcher, you will contribute to the development of AURORA resilient and circular strategies multi-scale assessment framework for designing circular and climate-resilient building construction and renovation pathways. Your research will focus on mapping and cataloguing innovative building technologies and investigating how individual products and product systems interact and can be combined into circular and resilient building configurations. Furthermore, you will contribute to the development of a digital database containing structured data for construction and renovation pathways, exploring how these can be adapted to different building typologies and hazard scenarios. You will then apply the developed framework to a Dutch urban neighborhood case-study.
Key activities include:
 Mapping integrated construction and renovation strategies, covering structural systems, façades and building systems equipment across different building typologies, climatic conditions and hazard contexts.
 Developing a catalogue of pre-evaluated configurations, supporting informed selection of resilient and circular construction and renovation options.
 Assisting in the integration of assessed technologies and pathways into decision-ready parametric datasets and a structured database, enabling direct integration into AURORA digital planning workflows.
 Applying the framework in real-time in a Dutch urban neighborhood.
You will collaborate with two research groups within the Faculty of Architecture and the Built Environment: Structures and Materials (restructgroup) and Building Design & Technology (architectural-facades-products), and one group within the Faculty of Civil Engineering and Geosciences: Hydraulic Structures and Flood Risk (hydraulic-structures-and-flood-risk). The position is funded for 48 months, during which the candidate will conduct doctoral research while contributing to the broader AURORA research program. The project offers opportunities to collaborate with leading European universities, industry partners, municipalities and public authorities working on circular construction, digital workflows and resilient urban development.
 Job requirements 
 You have a MSc degree in Building Sciences, such as Architectural Engineering, Building Technology, Civil Engineering, Environmental Engineering, or a related discipline;
 You have demonstrated knowledge of one or more of the following areas: circular construction, resilience analysis, building technologies, building performance;
 You have demonstrated experience in multi-scale approaches linking materials, components, buildings and urban systems and quantitative performance assessment methods;
 Knowledge of GIS, digital workflows or programming (e.g. Python) is an advantage;
 You have excellent oral and written communication skills in English. For more details, please check the Graduate Schools Admission Requirements.
 Knowledge of Dutch is considered a plus;
 You are able to work independently and as part of a team, and to build collaborative, interdisciplinary/transdisciplinary networks;
 You are motivated to develop innovative methods to support circular and resilient transformation of the built environment.
