PhD Replacing Chemicals with Electricity: Engineering Local pH Environments
Your job
 Can electricity replace acids, bases, and cleaning chemicals used throughout industry today? How do local pH conditions develop near electrodes and membranes in electrochemical systems, and how can they be controlled? In this PhD project, you will investigate these questions by combining modelling and experimental data to develop electrically driven alternatives for industrial cleaning and separation processes. 
 What will you do? 
 Many industries rely on acids, bases, detergents, and other chemicals to clean equipment, recover valuable products, and produce high-quality process water. These chemicals increase environmental impact, complicate water re-use and require downstream treatment. In this project, we take a different approach: rather than adding chemicals, we aim to create the required chemical conditions directly using electricity.
 A key challenge in replacing these chemicals with electricity is that electrochemical systems create localized pH environments near electrodes and membranes. These local conditions often differ strongly from bulk solution properties, yet they determine chemical speciation, surface interactions, selectivity, cleaning efficiency, and fouling behavior. The aim of this PhD project is to understand, predict, and engineer these local pH environments in electrochemical systems.
 As a PhD candidate, you will investigate how local pH environments develop near electrodes and membranes in complex water matrices. You will integrate theory, modelling, and experiments to determine how local pH conditions develop, how they depend on water composition and material properties, and how they can be engineered for practical applications. The insights obtained in this project can be used to develop electrically driven, chemical-free technologies for industrial cleaning and separations.
 You will be part of the  Electrically-driven Chemical-free Operations (ECO) consortium , a collaboration between the Institute for Sustainable Process Technology, the University of Twente, TU Delft, the University of Groningen, the University of Copenhagen, Wageningen University & Research, and industrial partners from the food, chemical, paper, and water sectors.
 Your duties and responsibilities include:  
 investigate how electrically induced local pH environments develop in electrochemical systems;
 develop theoretical and computational models to predict local pH conditions in complex water matrices and investigate the impact of water composition, electrode materials, and membrane materials on pH conditions;
 design experiments to quantify local pH environments near electrodes and membranes and integrate experimental observations and modelling results to develop design principles for electrically driven processes;
 use the obtained insights to guide the design of electrochemical cleaning and separation technologies in close collaboration with the industrial partners in the consortium;
 present research results at consortium meetings, international conferences, and scientific workshops and publish findings in leading peer-reviewed scientific journals.
 You will work here 
 The research is embedded within the  Environmental Technology group . You will join the Electrified Interfaces group, a research group studying transport, reactions, and selectivity at charged interfaces in environmental technologies, including electrochemical systems, membrane processes, adsorption and ion-exchange materials. You will be supervised by Dr. Jouke Dykstra and Dr. Hanieh Bazyar from TU Delft. 
 Your qualities
 You are an enthusiastic and curious researcher who enjoys working on complex scientific challenges. You combine analytical thinking with creativity and have a strong interest in understanding fundamental processes at interfaces. You are a team player and open to collaborating in a consortium of other researchers and industrial partners, with regular consortium meetings. You can communicate your research to people with a broad, technical background, and you can contribute to defining your own research, in agreement with the consortium.
 You also possess:  
 a successfully completed MSc degree in Chemical Engineering, Water Technology, Environmental Technology, Physical Chemistry, Process Engineering, or Applied Physics, or a related discipline;
 demonstrated affinity with electrochemistry, transport phenomena, membrane processes, colloid and interface science, and/or water technology;
 experience with experimental methods, modelling, or both, and enthusiasm to combine theory and experiments;
 excellent English communication skills and the motivation to publish your work in leading scientific journals.

The Faculty of Science and the Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research (LACDR) are looking for a: 
 PhD candidate for the project “Modulation of inflammatory Dendritic cell subsets in atherosclerosis” 
Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease where atherosclerotic plaques develop in the larger arteries. Atherosclerosis is the underlying pathology of cardiovascular disease events such as myocardial infarction or stroke. Currently, treatment focusses on lipid-lowering interventions, which do not target the chronic inflammation that causes plaque instability and major acute cardiovascular events. Therefore, studying the immune cells that contribute to atherosclerotic plaque destabilization may lead to novel therapeutic targets and intervention strategies.
In this project, we aim to investigate how inflammatory myeloid cell populations, with a focus on dendritic cell subsets contribute to the progression of atherosclerosis. Dendritic cells act as directors of the immune response by activating T cells and may thus fuel the ongoing chronic inflammatory response in advanced atherosclerosis. We aim to investigate novel mechanisms and identify new targets for more targeted therapeutic intervention.
 What you will do 
The aim of your PhD project is to obtain novel knowledge regarding myeloid immune cells in cardiovascular disease, specifically in advanced atherosclerosis.
You will:
1) identify myeloid cell subsets, with a particular focus on dendritic cells, in advanced human atherosclerosis and associate these with patient characteristics
2) investigate the functional changes of different dendritic cell subsets in advanced atherosclerosis
3) identify proatherogenic dendritic cell subsets and validate potential therapeutic targets for intervention.
You will make use of available human atherosclerotic tissue and datasets, design and perform in vitro studies and validate findings in vivo .
 What you bring 
We are looking for an enthusiastic, bright, well-motivated and ambitious scientist:
 With a recent Master degree in Bio-Pharmaceutical/Bio-medical sciences, immunology, molecular biology, or a related field,
 Strong background in immunology and/or cardiovascular research,
 With experience with in vivo studies (artikel 9, proefdierkunde), spectral flow cytometry, single-cell sequencing (working in R), microscopical techniques and molecular biology is an advantage,
 English proficiency (verbally and written),
 Who is an independent and creative team player with good communicative skills.
 Where you will work 
The Faculty of Science at Leiden University is a world-class faculty where staff and students work together in a dynamic international environment. It is a faculty where personal and academic development are top priorities. Our people are committed to expand fundamental knowledge by curiosity and to look beyond the borders of their own discipline; their aim is to benefit science, and to make a contribution to addressing the major societal challenges of the future.
The research carried out at the Faculty of Science is very diverse, ranging from mathematics, information science, astronomy, physics, chemistry and bio-pharmaceutical sciences to biology and environmental sciences. The research activities are organized in eight institutes. These institutes offer eight bachelors’ and twelve master’s programmes. The faculty has grown strongly in recent years and now has more than 2,700 staff and over 6,000 students. We are located at the heart of Leiden’s Bio Science Park, one of Europe’s biggest science parks, where university and business life come together.
The division of BioTherapeutics operates at the forefront of research in the field of therapeutic modulation of cardiovascular disease. The research aims to identify new immune targets in atherosclerosis and to develop innovative biopharmaceutical concepts to intervene in cardiovascular disease. The use of specific gene-knockout technology, biologics such as vaccines, therapeutic proteins and cellular therapy, provides a unique approach for the development of new therapies for the treatment or prevention of atherosclerosis. Are you fascinated by the influence of nature on our emotions and behaviour? Passionate about nature-inspired facade design and its influence on occupant comfort and wellbeing? Eager to embark on a multidisciplinary research project and collaborate with industry partners? If so, then this PhD position might be perfect for you.
 Information 
Can we reduce stress, thermal discomfort and energy consumption for cooling in homes by harnessing visual exposure to nature-inspired facade designs? Can we disentangle the beneficial effects of daylight and nature exposure through windows? How can we best navigate the trade-off between access to view and the amount and quality of daylight and nature content provided by a nature-inspired façade? These are some of the scientific challenges you will work on in this PhD project.
This PhD position is part of the wider ΝWO KIC project “Nature4Homes: Nature-driven building skin interventions for energy efficiency, occupant comfort, health, and biodiversity in dwellings”, which brings together the domains of building engineering, building physics, environmental psychology, meteorology, and thermophysiology to develop nature-driven building skin solutions that enhance occupant health and comfort while reducing cooling demand. This PhD project focuses specifically on the domains of environmental psychology, lighting research, and building physics.
You will conduct your research within the Human-Technology Interaction group (HTI) at TU/e, which has a long history in lighting research and environmental psychology, with a secondment at the Environmental & Climate Design section at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), which has extensive expertise in building physics and indoor environmental quality.
In this PhD, you will investigate whether visual patterns from nature across different layers of the building skin (e.g., the façade itself, the view to the outside) within an occupant’s field of view can support mental wellbeing, increase acceptance, and enhance tolerance to visual and thermal discomfort indoors, particularly during periods of summer overheating. To address these questions, you will review the literature, perform experiments in virtual reality and real conditions, co-create nature-inspired façade elements, and test them in field studies. Your work would include collecting self-reported, physiological, and environmental data, and apply building simulation, computer vision, and advanced statistical methods for their analysis. The project also involves close collaboration with industry partners such as shading system manufacturers to develop nature-inspired façade interventions. These will be tested at the “Green Village” living lab housing of TU Delft. Throughout your PhD, you will be supervised by Dr. Kynthia Chamilothori (main supervisor) and Prof. Yvonne de Kort (promotor) at the Human-Technology Interaction group of the Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e), as well as Dr. Eleonora Brembilla (co-promotor) at the Environmental & Climate Design section at TU Delft. You will be based at TU/e with a secondment at TU Delft.

REQUIREMENTS:
A master’s degree (or an equivalent university degree) in environmental psychology, lighting research, architectural or building engineering, or human-technology interaction.
 Proficiency in experimental research with human participants and quantitative data analysis, along with experience or eagerness to learn building simulation, façade technologies and programming.
 A research-oriented attitude.
 Ability to work in an interdisciplinary team and interest in collaborating with industrial partners.
 Motivated to develop your teaching skills and coach students.
 Fluent in spoken and written English (C1 level).

CONTRACT: 4 years

Your job
 PFAS are among the most challenging contaminants facing drinking water utilities worldwide. Although granular activated carbon (GAC) is widely applied for PFAS removal, utilities face challenges with rapid PFAS breakthrough and  as a consequence  more frequent re-activation of activated carbon filters. The factors controlling breakthrough under realistic drinking water conditions remain insufficiently understood, particularly in the presence of natural organic matter (NOM) in the water matrix. 
 As a PhD candidate, you will investigate how water composition, natural organic matter, and activated carbon properties influence PFAS removal in drinking water treatment. You will combine laboratory experiments, column studies, and data analysis to identify the factors governing PFAS breakthrough at environmentally relevant conditions and concentrations.
 Working closely with drinking water company Evides, you will study PFAS adsorption in realistic drinking water matrices and evaluate how differences in NOM composition affect filter performance. The insights obtained in this project will support the development of improved operational strategies for activated carbon filtration and help drinking water utilities better predict and manage PFAS breakthrough in practice.
 Your duties and responsibilities include:  
 investigating the mechanisms governing competitive adsorption of PFAS and natural organic matter on granular activated carbon;
 designing and conducting batch and column experiments at environmentally relevant PFAS concentrations;
 analysing experimental data and developing predictive tools for activated carbon filter performance;
 identifying key water quality parameters that can serve as indicators for PFAS breakthrough;
 publishing your results in international scientific journals and presenting your work at conferences.

Description 
 ORFeus is a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Network, funded by Horizon Europe (Grant Agreement No. 101309891) and coordinated by the Princess Máxima Center for Pediatric Oncology in Utrecht. It is recruiting 15 doctoral candidates for PhD projects starting in March 2027.
 The science 
 Thousands of small open reading frames (smORFs), many in transcripts classed as non-coding, are translated into microproteins that standard genome annotation and proteomics miss. ORFeus aims to find these proteins, understand how their translation is regulated and what they do, and test their relevance for cancer and immunology.
 The projects 
 The 15 projects are hosted at 14 institutions in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Germany, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Norway, and Switzerland. They range from fully experimental to fully computational:
 Discovery and annotation (DC1 to DC5): machine learning for cross-species smORF prediction, single-molecule translation mapping with nanopore sequencing, rare translation events, microprotein interactions in bacterial infection, and capture of secreted microproteins by crosslinking mass spectrometry
 Function and regulation (DC6 to DC10): computational design of microprotein binders, lncRNA translation in human neurons, evolutionary analysis of new genes, single-cell translation after base editing, and thermal proteome profiling
 Cancer and immunology (DC11 to DC15): smORF-derived antigens in HPV-driven cancer, genetic variation in smORFs, stress-induced codon substitutions as neoepitopes, CRISPR screens for antigen presentation, and HLA presentation of cryptic peptides
 What we offer 
 Full-time, 36-month employment contracts with full social security under MSCA conditions, with a living allowance (adjusted by the host country's correction coefficient), a mobility allowance and, where applicable, a family allowance. Each doctoral candidate enrolls in a PhD program, spends around three months on a secondment with an industry or research partner, and joins a network-wide training program of schools, workshops and conferences.
 Who we are looking for 
 Candidates with a master's degree (or equivalent) in molecular biology, biochemistry, genetics, bioinformatics, computational biology, computer science, immunology, or a related field. MSCA eligibility rules apply: no doctoral degree, and no more than 12 months spent in the host country in the 36 months before recruitment. Any nationality may apply.
 How to apply 
 Candidates can apply to up to three projects. Full project descriptions, supervisor details, eligibility information and application forms are available via the application link on this posting. Applications close on 22 October 2026, 23:59 CET.

By combining electron optics, MEMS technology, experimental microscopy, and computational imaging, we aim to open new possibilities for high-resolution surface imaging at low electron energies.
As the postdoctoral researcher, you will take the technical and scientific ownership of the instrument development, from electron-optical design through to fabrication, integration and experimental demonstration. You will work closely with two PhD candidates with complimentary roles: one will focus on experimental imaging, microscope characterization, and establishing the imaging methodology, while the other will develop computational imaging approaches and apply them to surface science. You will also work closely with the PI and an electron-optics technician supporting the project.
A central challenge is to develop compact electron-optical components that can separate the desired coherent backscattered-electron signal from the primary beam and direct it towards a dedicated detector. You will design and characterize these components, coordinate their fabrication and integration, and lead the commisioning and optimization of the experimental instrument.
Your work will span electron-optical design, electromagnetic and ray-tracing simulations, MEMS and nanofabrication, vacuum technology, detector integration and experimental microscopy. Working with the experimental-imaging PhD candidate, you will establish the performance of the instrument and the conditions needed to acquire high-quality diffraction data. You will also work with computational-imaging PhD candidate to connect the experimental measurements to reconstruction and imaging methods.

PhD Researcher in Atmospheric Sciences - Emerging extreme fire weather risks
Your job
 Are you a meteorologist or climate scientist with a passion to investigate the interactions between climate extremes and wildfire risks? Do you want to work on a research project that aims to understand the most extreme fire weather events possible, and how they will evolve in a warming world? Then this position may be the perfect opportunity for you! 
 The Meteorology and Air Quality (MAQ) Group at Wageningen University and Research is looking for a PhD candidate with a background in meteorology, atmospheric or climate sciences to work on unprecedented and emerging fire weather risks.
 Extreme fire weather, referring to the meteorological component of fire risk that reflects the combined effects of heat, drought, wind, and atmospheric aridity, is one of the key factors influencing wildfire spread and intensity. Climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of fire weather extremes across many regions, including the Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes. Therefore, understanding and anticipating the most intense, persistent or otherwise most impactful fire weather conditions plausible today, as well as how these conditions may worsen under future warming, is crucial for fire risk assessment and preparedness. What are worst-case fire weather conditions possible under current climate versus in a warmer world, what atmospheric or climatic mechanisms drive them, and how this relates to actual fire occurrence and behaviour, are all questions that will be addressed within this PhD project. To answer them, you will investigate the most extreme events in the historical record and how they compare to the most extreme events in state-of-the-art climate modelling experiments. 
 This project will be supervised by Dr. Laura Suarez-Gutierrez in collaboration with Prof. Guido van der Werf and carried out in the highly multidisciplinary setting of the MAQ group. You will join a thriving, highly collaborative research environment with leading expertise in weather and climate extremes, fire dynamics, and their interactions.
 Your qualities
 You hold a MSc degree in meteorology, atmospheric sciences, climate sciences, physics, engineering, or related field;
 You are passionate about understanding climate extremes and fire risks;
 You are enthusiastic and motivated to work on this research project with independence as well as in a collaborative environment
 You are experienced in handling large data sets, for example weather and/or climate model and/or satellite data; 
 You have good programming skills (Python, shell scripts, and/or comparable experience);
 Prior knowledge and research experience in weather and climate extremes, fire risk, atmospheric and climate dynamics, and/or climate modelling is valued.

PhD: 3D radiation in clouds and wildfire plumes using GPUs and machine learning
Your job
 This PhD project is part of ORCRIST: Optimized Ray-tracing for Cloud-Radiation Interaction Simulations in 3D using GPUs and Machine Learning, funded by the NWO Open Technology Programme.
 Sunlight and heat radiation move through the atmosphere in three dimensions, yet almost every weather and climate model still treats radiation as a purely vertical process. We want to change that. As a PhD candidate in Wageningen, you will help build the first Monte Carlo ray tracer for the atmosphere that is fast enough for forecasting, and use it to find out how 3D radiation shapes clouds, solar energy availability, climate sensitivity and wildfire plumes. You will work in a tandem with a fellow PhD student in computer science at Leiden University, who focuses on GPU optimization, while you lead the physics. Together you will develop a machine-learning denoiser that brings the ray tracer to operational speed. Your research has a clear route to society: throughout the project you will work with a user committee of KNMI, weather forecasting company Whiffle, TNO, software company VORtech and Columbia University. 
 Your duties and responsibilities include:  
 Setting up three benchmark simulations in the GPU-accelerated model MicroHH: solar energy forecasting, tropical climate, and a real wildfire plume.
 Developing a 3D thermal radiation solver within the RTE-RRTMGP-CPP ray tracer, including smart strategies for sampling radiation sources.
 Quantifying how 3D radiation changes clouds, surface irradiance and plume dynamics compared to conventional 1D radiation.
 Co-developing a physics-informed machine-learning denoiser with your Leiden colleague, and evaluating it together with the user committee in operational settings.
 Publishing your results in leading journals and presenting them at international conferences and to users from the field. 
 You will work here 
 The research is embedded within the chair of Meteorology ( Meteorology and Air Quality Group ), led by Prof. Vilà-Guerau de Arellano. You will be supervised by Dr.ir. Chiel van Heerwaarden and Dr.ir. Menno Veerman, both at WUR, and by Dr. Ben van Werkhoven at Leiden University. The team is small, open and collaborative, and has a track record of building widely used open-source simulation codes. Your job
 We are looking for a talented Post-Doctoral Researcher for a 1- to 2-years position for the development of AFM-IR infrared nanospectroscopy in combination with microfluidics to achieve chemical analysis of protein and their assemblies in liquid physiological conditions. 
 As a post-doctoral researcher, you will contribute to push the boundaries of nano-chemical analysis, withing the Ruggeri’s lab at Wageningen University in the frame of the project  Nano-Scope . 
 The Nano-Scope project focuses on the study of protein interactions and self-assembly in disease and drug formulations at the single-molecule level; and it runs in collaboration with dr. Ioana Ilie at Amsterdam University, as well as several industrial partners: Bruker Nano (USA); Digital Surf (France); Novo Nordisk (Denmark); Discoveric Bio Alpha (Switzerland).
 Your duties and responsibilities include:  
 developing and applying nano-chemical imaging and spectroscopy via AFM-IR to study protein structure and chemical properties;

 writing manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed scientific journals reporting on the results of your research;
 supervising MSc and PhD students.
 Your team 
 You will work with  dr Francesco Simone Ruggeri and his team of Nanoscale Imaging and Spectroscopy, which will include several PhDs and Post-Doctoral researchers. The group develops and applies advanced nanoscale imaging and spectroscopy approaches to investigate the chemical, structural, and physical properties of complex molecular systems.
 You will work here

Do you want to contribute to ethnographic research into the politics of valuing seaweed in Scotland? 
The Leiden University's Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology, based within the Faculty of Social Sciences, is looking for an ambitious PhD-candidate to study the impacts of economization of seaweed as part of ‘blue economy’ strategies in Scotland. Research focuses on the impacts on coastal communities considering that in Scotland colonial legacies still influence patterns of unequal access to and use of coastal areas. You will work within the project ‘Entangled in seaweed: The politics of economising nature in Scotland and South Africa’ funded by an NWO Open Competition grant.
 Project Description 
The project investigates the impacts of economisation of seaweed as part of a global drive to develop ‘blue economy’ strategies. Seaweed harvesting and cultivation (as food, or fertilizer- and bioplastic ingredient) are increasing considerably and promoted as contributing to sustainable development. The project focuses on coastal communities in Scotland, which has developed a comprehensive blue economy strategy. Building on insights from political ecology and valuation studies and inspired by the multispecies turn in anthropology, this project aims to study local impacts of new forms of economisation of seaweed, and the possible contestations these may entail. It seeks to incorporate the ideas, interests, and knowledge from local groups who live from, in and with seaweed ecologies, examining how new versions of economisation affect local social relations, including the entanglements with non-humans these ecologies and economisations depend on. It does so by focusing on valuations of seaweed ecologies, based on an understanding of values as enacted through practices by all (human and non-human) stakeholders. The project employs a collaborative approach vis-à-vis research participants and a wider audience through a visual storytelling approach.
 What you will do 
You will work in a project team consisting of two PhD-candidates and researchers at Leiden University, collaborating with project partners in Scotland. You will:
 Develop a research proposal in the context of the overall project theme, and conduct twelve months of ethnographic research in Scotland. An ethics review and contribution to the data management plan are included in the proposal development. Research includes historical document/policy analysis, participant observation, interviews, and the application of participatory visual storytelling methods.
 Analyse research findings and write a dissertation that contributes to the objectives of the ‘Entangled with Seaweed’ project.
 Actively contribute to the output and dissemination of the research project, which includes collaborating with the other team members on academic and non-academic publications, science communication, and the organisation of workshops, seminars and an exhibition.
 Participate in relevant PhD-courses and masterclasses, organised in accordance with the guidelines of the Faculty of Social Science and the Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology. PhD-courses at the University of Edinburgh, our partner in the project, can be included in the individual training and supervision plan as well.
 Participate in the PhD programme and other academic activities of the Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology at Leiden University. During your stay in Scotland you will also be able to participate in the PhD-programme at the University of Edinburgh as well as academic activities organised by the Scottish Association for Marine Science (SAMS).
 Where you will work 
The Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences consists of five institutes: the Centre for Science and Technology Studies, Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology, Education and Child Studies, Political Science, and Psychology. The faculty is home to approximately 7,000 students and 1,000 staff members. Our institutes are dedicated not only to education but also to groundbreaking research that expands our understanding of human behavior and societal structures. What makes our faculty unique is the diversity of research topics, the variety of teaching approaches, and the structure of professional support. This provides you with the opportunity to explore and develop your interests and expertise. For an introduction to our faculty, visit our website: Welcome to the Leiden Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences – Leiden University .
 Leiden University's Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology (CADS) 
Leiden University's Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology concentrates on 'global vulnerability and social resilience'. The institute has three main themes: diversity, sustainability, and digitalisation. We are looking to hire people who have refugee status in The Netherlands and who are completing (or have recently completed) civic integration ( inburgering ) to join an academic research team at Tilburg University. In this project, we are interested in the ways that refugees use digital technologies (such as translation tools, government apps, and chatbots) to help manage the civic integration process, including the barriers and opportunities of technology. As a research assistant, you will participate as an active team member, providing input and playing a role in key stages of the research process (design, recruitment, data collection, analysis). You will offer your insights as someone with firsthand experience of civic integration as well as contribute your interpersonal and language skills for recruitment and data collection. No previous research experience is required.
 Why should someone apply for this job?  In this position, you will gain experience conducting academic research, working on a professional team in The Netherlands, and contributing to solutions for technological challenges that refugees face during civic integration.
 Why do we seek the expertise of refugees for this research? We believe we can better understand the challenges that refugees face in The Netherlands by working closely with people who have that firsthand experience. By hiring research assistants who have experience as refugees, we hope to identify more relevant questions, engage in more responsible ways with the community, and develop findings that more impactful for improving the lives of refugees.
 Your position 
 Research assistant.
 Job responsibilities include the following: 
 Attend orientation and training sessions on basic research skills (no previous research experience required).
 Participate in regular team meetings, weekly or every two weeks on average, in person in Tilburg (remote attendance possible on occasion).
 Contribute to the development of research questions and study design through feedback on proposed ideas and designs.
 Assist in recruiting participants through, e.g., distributing recruitment materials and helping contact potential participants through community organizations and refugee networks.
 Assist in data collection by serving as a co-moderator/co-interviewer for focus groups/interviews alongside the lead researcher, including providing translation as needed.
 Assist in analyzing data collected from focus groups or interviews through reading transcripts and participating in team meetings to provide input on analysis.
 Contribute to communicating research findings to the public through feedback on the planning of, and/or participation in, community events or stakeholder meetings.
 Assist in communication with participants (i.e., translation) throughout the research process, including during recruitment, scheduling, and data collection.

ADDITIONAL INFORMATION:

 Employment of 0.1 fte (4 hours per week).
 The research assistant position will be ranked in the Dutch university job ranking system (UFO) as a research assistant 1.
 Salary of €314.70 gross per month for this 0,1 fte employment (UFO-profile Research Assistant 1, salary scale 5). Tilburg University uses a neutral remuneration system based on relevant work experience.
 This is a vacancy whose work is temporarily funded on the basis of temporary external funding or co-financing, in accordance with Article 2.3 paragraph 5 sub a CLA DU, namely NWO XS Grant “Participatory Approach to Digital Inclusion for Refugees in The Netherlands”. You will be given a temporary contract for the duration of 9 months.
 Vacation pay of 8% and a year-end bonus of 8.3%.
 Over 8 weeks of vacation leave.
 Reimbursement sustainable commuting: walking, cycling, and public transport.
 Options model for additional leave, pension, a bicycle or personal training.

Faculty:  Faculty of Veterinary Medicine Department:  Department Population Health Sciences Hours per week:  36 to 40 Application deadline:  25 October 2026
This PhD position will advance our knowledge regarding environmental pesticide exposure and cognition in children. The project does two things: It analyses biomonitoring data of pesticide exposure with tests of brain function of the children. It also examines the full Dutch population to understand risks of pesticide exposure to cognitive development and school functioning in children. Childhood cognitive development shapes health and success later in life, understanding how environmental risk factors alter children's brain function, learning and behaviour matters well beyond childhood.
 Your job
 Pesticides are applied to crops to protect them from weeds, insects, fungi and other pests that reduce yield. Because they're used widely around the world, people are exposed to them chronically. This has raised concerns about health effects, especially for people who live close to treated fields.
 In this project, we collect data from children taking part in the national OBO2 study. We use biomonitoring to measure their current pesticide exposure and link it to their brain function, which we assess with a test battery. We also apply geospatial exposure estimates developed within the OBO2 consortium to the school results of all children in the Netherlands. In your PhD project, you'll analyse both data sources to investigate possible health effects of pesticide exposure. Two methodological challenges run through both studies. Children are exposed to many pesticides at once, so you'll use mixture modelling to estimate their combined effects rather than looking at one compound at a time. And because the data follow children and exposures over several years, you'll apply longitudinal methods to study how exposure relates to cognition and school performance over time. We're looking for a candidate with a strong background in epidemiology and quantitative methods, solid programming experience in R.
 The project is part of a national research program on pesticides and health. For the analyses of child cognition, you’ll be part of a team of researchers, including other (PhD) students and external collaborators involved in the OBO-2 project ( https://www.bestrijdingsmiddelen-omwonenden.nl/over-onderzoeken ). You'll work within the dynamic One Health Chemical (OHC) group, which is performing interdisciplinary research to uncover environmental health determinants.
 Your qualities
 We are looking for a candidate that meets the following criteria:
 A recently completed or nearly completed Master's degree in epidemiology or a related discipline that prepared you for conducting the research outlined in this project.
 Experience with quantitative methods (e.g., experiments, surveys) to quantify factors relevant to human health.
 Solid background in epidemiological study designs and methodological aspects, for example through academic research projects or a master’s thesis.
 Good knowledge in using R.
 Strong communication skills in English, both written and spoken.
 Good knowledge of Dutch language.
 Demonstrated critical thinking skills and the ability to collaborate effectively within an interdisciplinary research environment.
 Our offer
 A position for initially one year, with an extension to a total of four years upon a positive assessment in the first one year;
 a gross monthly salary starting at €3204 in the first year and increasing annually up to €4051 in the fourth year, based on full-time employment (salary scale P under the Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Universities (CAO NU));
 8% holiday pay and 8.3% year-end bonus;
 a pension scheme, partially paid parental leave and flexible terms of employment based on the CAO NU (more information about working at Utrecht University can be found here https://www.uu.nl/en/organisation/working-at-utrecht-university).
 About us
 At IRAS we collaborate internationally to improve the health of humans and their environment. IRAS is a world-leading institute in the research field of exposure assessment in the (work) environment and related health effects. We develop and apply advanced methods to further improve the research in this field. The international character of IRAS is also reflected in its employees who originate from all over the world.
 A better future for everyone. This ambition motivates our scientists in executing their leading research and inspiring teaching. At  Utrecht University , the various disciplines collaborate intensively towards major  strategic themes . Our focus is on Dynamics of Youth, Institutions for Open Societies, Life Sciences and Pathways to Sustainability.  Sharing science, shaping tomorrow .

We are committed to creating a safe and inclusive environment where everyone can thrive and contribute. Read more about our commitment to diversity and inclusion. If you have any questions about accessibility, for example regarding your workplace Nieuw Gildestein , the application process or your work, please contact us via our HR contact page .

MERIT (MEtabolic Reprogramming in viral pathogenesis: from Infection to Therapeutic innovations) is an EU-funded MSCA training programme aimed at better understanding how viruses affect the human body. Coordinated by Dr. Adithya Sridhar, Assistant Professor, and Prof. Dr. Dasja Pajkrt, Professor of Pediatric Infectious diseases, from the OrganoVIR Labs at Amsterdam UMC (location AMC), this project brings together 7 academic institutions and 12 associated partners from across Europe.
 Within MERIT, researchers will take a new, holistic approach that focuses on infections and host metabolism to unravel virus-induced metabolic reprogramming and its impact on human health. The project’s objective lies in understanding the complex interplay between viruses and host cells, focusing on metabolic reprogramming, and long-term consequences of infection. This will be achieved by combining three methodological pillars: human organoids, integrative and spatial omics, and advanced microscopy.
 Role of mitochondrial dysfunction in enterovirus CNS disease
 Tailoring and implementing strategies for safe virus research in EU laboratories
 Understanding the consequences of common cold coronavirus infection in the lung on the CNS
 Understanding long-term alterations in the CNS following common cold coronavirus infections
 Multi-modal microscopy and tomography of viral infections in organoids
 Molecular fingerprinting in organoids using Raman and autofluorescence micro-spectroscopy
 Mechanisms of HIV-induced neurodegeneration
 Elucidating the role of host lipoprotein receptors in alphavirus infections
 Alphavirus interplay with host lipid homeostasis in CNS organoids
 Genotype-specific metabolic footprint in human EV infections along the gut-brain axis
 Role of lipid metabolism in virus-induced neurodenegeration
 Immunometabolic engineering for next-generation alphavirus therapeutics
 Role of macrophages in lung cancer-infection niche
 SARS-CoV-2 persistent and PLpro-mediated reprogramming in the context of long COVID
 Immunometabolism and metabolic engineering for a functional HIV cure

euraxess:472213.description:
Je hebt nog 30 dag(en) om te solliciteren 
 Contribute to the MERIT project and investigate how viral infections affect lipid metabolism and virus-induced neurodegeneration. As a doctoral candidate MERIT Project at LUMC, you will work with advanced mass spectrometry techniques and focus on lipid biosynthetic pathways in neurons and glial cells. You will be part of an EU-funded MSCA training programme that brings together academic institutions and partners from across Europe. Planned secondments and network-wide training opportunities allow you to further develop your scientific and professional skills. 
Wat ga je doen? 
 At the Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC), MERIT is looking for a doctoral candidate to work on Work Packages 1 and 2. As DC11, you will investigate how viral infections affect lipid biosynthetic pathways and explore the therapeutic targeting of lipid metabolism for controlling virus-induced neurodegeneration.
 Your objectives are:
 Understand how viral infections modulate lipid biosynthetic pathways in neurons and glial cells.
 Identify specific lipid classes, species and metabolites affected by viral infections.
 Investigate the therapeutic targeting of lipid metabolism for controlling virus-induced neurodegeneration.
 You will be guided during your research project by dr. Elena Sanchez Lopez, dr. Nina Ogrinc and prof. dr. Martin Giera.
Waar ga je werken? 
 MERIT (MEtabolic Reprogramming in viral pathogenesis: from Infection to Therapeutic innovations) is an EU-funded MSCA training programme aimed at better understanding how viruses affect the human body. Coordinated by dr. Adithya Sridhar, Assistant Professor, and prof. dr. Dasja Pajkrt, Professor of Pediatric Infectious Diseases, from the OrganoVIR Labs at Amsterdam UMC (location AMC), this project brings together seven academic institutions and 12 associated partners from across Europe.
 Within MERIT, researchers will take a new, holistic approach that focuses on infections and host metabolism to unravel virus-induced metabolic reprogramming and its impact on human health. The project’s objective lies in understanding the complex interplay between viruses and host cells, focusing on metabolic reprogramming and the long-term consequences of infection. This will be achieved by combining three methodological pillars: human organoids, integrative and spatial omics, and advanced microscopy.
 The Center for Proteomics and Metabolomics (CPM) at LUMC is the technological expertise center and innovation partner of the LUMC in the analysis of proteins, metabolites, lipids and glycan structures from biological materials such as cells and tissues. Mass spectrometry is the core technology within CPM and is complemented by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and advanced miniaturised separation techniques. You will join the Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry Imaging groups.
Wat neem je mee? 
 About you
 An interest in working in a multidisciplinary research group is important for this position. You communicate clearly in English and enjoy working with researchers from different backgrounds and areas of expertise.
 Furthermore, you have:
 A master's degree in analytical chemistry, biomedical sciences or related fields.
 Practical experience with mass spectrometry (LC-MS and/or MALDI-MS-based techniques).
 Preferably, experience with data processing and analysis.
 Excellent oral and written communication skills in English (minimum C1/C2 CEFR level).
 Our offer 
 A contract with LUMC for 36 hours per week for four years.
 A gross monthly salary ranging from € 3,217 to € 4,077 (scale PRO, CAO UMC).
 A salary increase of 3.5% will take effect on 1 May 2027.
 Planned secondments at Amsterdam University Medical Center and Medical University Innsbruck.
 Training in safety and biosecurity aligned with international best practices. You will be trained in hazard identification, containment, incident reporting and dual-use/gain-of-function issues.
 The opportunity to take part in a tailor-made pre-MBA programme to develop entrepreneurial and commercial skills and other network-wide training opportunities, including conferences and courses, a Personal Development Plan, non-academic coaching, and workshops on ethics, sustainability and AI/LLM.
 You must not have resided, carried out work or studied in the Netherlands for more than 12 months in the 36 months immediately before 1 April 2027.
 You are entitled to an end-of-year bonus (8.3%), holiday allowance, a bicycle scheme, sports allowance, home-working compensation and an excellent commuting reimbursement scheme. As an employee of LUMC, you will also be enrolled in the ABP pension fund. This means that 70% of your pension contribution is paid by LUMC.
 Meer informatie 
 •    You can apply for this position until 30 October 2026. Applications submitted after this date will not be considered.
•    Applications must be submitted via the application form on MERIT’s website. Only applications submitted via MERIT’s website will be considered.

Faculty:  Faculty of Veterinary Medicine Department:  Department Biomolecular Health Sciences Hours per week:  36 to 40 Application deadline:  31 October 2026
PhD position in a novel cell secretome-based therapeutics for osteoarthritis 
 Faculty: Faculty of Veterinary Medicine
 Department: Department of Biomolecular Health Sciences
 Hours per week: 36 to 40
 Application deadline: 31 October 2026
 Your job
 This PhD project will tackle key challenges in developing new therapies based on Extracellular Vesicles(EV)-enriched scretomes. The aim of the research is to develop innovative technologies that can be used to monitor batch-to-batch consistency of EV-based therapeutics, decipher EV- molecular cargo - functional relationships, and identify disease-related signatures in blood and synovial fluid from patients with osteoarthritis. Overall, the project aims to provide new insights and tools for the development of safe, effective, and consistent EV-based therapies.
 In this project hands-on analytical wet-lab experiments, including cell biological analyses, multi-omics mass spectrometry and nanoparticle analyses of EV samples, production batches and patients samples, as well as computational methods including AI-enhanced analyses are equally important. Throughout the project, you will develop core skills in fundamental cell biology and metabolism research, in mass spectrometry and integrated multi-omics analysis, and gain insights in the mechanism of action of EV-enriched cell secretome therapy in osteoarthritis. As part of an EU-funded RIA project in a 10-partner consortium including industry partnerships, you will collaborate with partner institutes in The Netherlands and abroad,  and secondments are possible. 
 Your qualities
 A relevant Master’s degree in Biology, Biomedical sciences, Biopharmaceutical Sciences, Biochemistry, or a related field, and a solid background in one or more of the following areas: cell biology, metabolism, immune regulation or joint biology;
 A strong interest in fundamental cell biology and hands-on analytical wet-lab techniques;
 Enthusiasm for nanoparticle analysis and the application of advanced technologies, such as high-resolution flow cytometry and optical fingerprinting;
 A strong interest in mass spectrometry and its applications in metabolomics, lipidomics, and proteomics. Experience with multi-omics analyses is an advantage;
 Basic proficiency in data analysis using R, Python, and/or Matlab, with a strong interest in computational methods, including AI-enhanced analyses;
 Excellent skills in writing and speaking English (C1 level);
 Interest in multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary research, reaching from fundamental to applied clinical research and from academic to industrial research;
 Ability to work as part of an interdisciplinary research consortium, with strong communication skills and interest to engage effectively with different groups (Academic & Clinical researchers, engineers, bio-informaticians and Industrial partners)
 Our offer
 a job for 12 months, with an extension to a total of four years upon a successful assessment in the first year, and with the specific intent that it results in a doctorate within this period;
 a working week of 36 - 40 hours and a gross monthly salary between €3.204 and €4.051 (salary scale P under the Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Universities (CAO NU)). The salary is based on a 38-hour working week;
 8% holiday pay and 8.3% year-end bonus;
 a pension scheme, partially paid parental leave and flexible terms of employment based on the CAO NU.
 In addition to the terms of employment set out in our collective labour agreement, we offer attractive additional benefits, including opportunities for  personal and professional growth , flexible leave arrangements, and extra vacation days. Through the UU Terms of Employment Options Model, you can tailor your employment package to your needs. In this way, we encourage you to grow in what you do, both in your work and in your development. Read more about  our terms of employment .
 About us
 A better future for everyone. This ambition motivates our scientists in executing their leading research and inspiring teaching. At  Utrecht University , the various disciplines collaborate intensively towards major  strategic themes . Our focus is on Dynamics of Youth, Institutions for Open Societies, Life Sciences and Pathways to Sustainability.  Sharing science, shaping tomorrow .
 At the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine we train the veterinarians and researchers of the future, provide care for animals and conduct leading and societal relevant research. That is what we are good at. We see that the health and welfare of animals, humans and the environment are interconnected. By sharing our knowledge and working together, we make positive impact, both nationally and internationally. Our 1,500 students and 950 staff members inspire and strengthen each other. Our engagement connects us. The drive to, from an integral perspective, make the world a better place.
 The Department of Biomolecular Health Sciences consists of the Divisions of Pathology, Infectious Diseases & Immunology and the Division of Cell Biology, Metabolism and Cancer (CMC), and hosts the centralized research facilities: Centre for Cell Imaging, Flow Cytometry and Cell Sorting and the Metabolism Expertise Center. The research of the Division CMC aims to unravel mechanisms of intra- and extracellular communication of animal cells. This knowledge is used to prevent or to develop better treatments for non-communicable diseases in veterinary and human patients. The Cell Biology section, headed by prof. dr. Marca Wauben, aims to decipher fundamental principles of cell-derived vesicle(EV)-mediated communication in health and disease processes. This research spans from fundamental discovery to translational applications, and the development of cutting-edge technology and methodology for tailored EV-research solutions. The Cancer Metabolism section, headed by prof. dr. Celia Berkers and prof. dr. Bernd Helms,  studies metabolic alterations and metabolic cross-talk in cancer, with the aim to identify novel metabolic targets for therapy. To achieve this, the team develops and applies advanced model systems and metabolomic, lipidomics and isotope tracing analyses, combined with biochemical and cell biological approaches. 
 For more information about the Cell Biology and Cancer Metabolism Sections

 For more information about this position, please contact Prof. Marca Wauben by email  m.h.m.wauben@uu.nl or Prof. Celia Berkers by email at c.r.berkers@uu.nl

Welcome to Maastricht University! 
We have developed a new class of oncology drugs that exploit the tumour microenvironment for selective activation that target the NOTCH stem-cell pathway in cancer. We are looking for an ambitious postdoctoral researcher to establish their therapeutic potential in advanced in vivo cancer models. You will determine efficacy, mechanism of action and tumour-microenvironment responses, and investigate how these drugs can improve treatment when combined with standard-of-care therapies and immunotherapy.
 Postdoctoral Researcher – Preclinical Cancer Drug Development 
 Our goal: We are developing a new class of tumour-selective small-molecule drugs targeting the NOTCH pathway, designed to become activated only within the tumour microenvironment. By restricting drug activity to tumours, we aim to target treatment-resistant cancer cells while limiting exposure and toxicity in healthy tissues. Our initial disease focus is triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), where we will determine efficacy as monotherapy and in rational combinations with established cancer treatments. The broader objective is to establish a tumour-specific precision-oncology platform that can subsequently be applied to other difficult-to-treat cancers.
 Your colleagues: You will join the group of Marc Vooijs in the Radiotherapy department at Maastricht University and Maastro Radiation Institute, working in a multidisciplinary environment spanning basic and translational cancer biology, including expertise in stem cell biology, tumour metabolomics and vesicle biology and primary (patient) tissue culture models. You will collaborate with scientists and clinicians and contribute to a programme designed to bridge academic discovery to preclinical drug development. This is a 3-year Dutch Cancer Society (Alpe d’Huzes/KWF-funded) project starting on 01-01-2027.
 What you do 
 Design, perform and analyse in vivo breast-cancer studies, using immune-competent TNBC models.
 Establish drug dose, schedule and treatment conditions for drug-combination strategies, including chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immunotherapy.
 Quantify tumour response, tolerability and survival, and relate these to pharmacokinetics, tumour-selective drug activation and target engagement.
 Characterise treatment-induced changes in the tumour microenvironment, including tumour, vascular and immune responses, using molecular, histological and imaging approaches.
 Identify and validate pharmacodynamic and response biomarkers to support patient stratification and clinical translation.
 Communicate results through project meetings, scientific presentations and high-quality publications and contribute scientifically to subsequent translational studies and funding applications.
 Support some teaching activities related to Oncology
 Are you ready to set the course for the years ahead? Then we’d love to meet you. 
 What you bring 
We are looking for a motivated biomedical scientist who wants to use advanced cancer models to translate innovative biology into new therapeutic strategies. Do you recognise yourself in this?
 PhD in cancer biology, with a demonstrated track record of peer-reviewed publications in a relevant research area.
 Strong hands-on experience within vivo cancer models is essential, including experimental design, tumour-response assessment and tissue collection. A valid Article 9 qualification or equivalent is required.
 A strong interest in translational oncology, innovation and preclinical drug development is essential.
 Experience with the tumour immune microenvironment and/or immuno-oncology is preferred.
 Experience with molecular and -omics analysis of tumours is preferred, including transcriptomic, single-cell, spatial or related approaches and their integration with in vivo treatment response.
 Experience with combination treatments, pharmacology/PK-PD or radiotherapy is an advantage; Article 5B or equivalent irradiation certification is preferred.
 What we offer 
At Maastricht University, you’ll work in an international, open, and engaged environment. We offer:
 A 12-month contract (1,0 FTE) with the prospect of a two-year extension.
 A gross monthly salary between €3.706 and €5.760 (based on full-time employment of 38 hours per week). 8% holiday allowance and an 8.3% year-end bonus.
 29 vacation days (based on full-time), four additional days off (Carnival Monday and Tuesday, Good Friday, and Liberation Day), and the possibility to accrue up to 12 extra days through compensation hours.
 A close-knit community of colleagues to collaborate and grow with.
 A solid pension plan via ABP, company fitness schemes, and access to various university sports facilities.
 An inspiring work environment in the heart of Europe.

euraxess:472220.description:
Are you a highly motivated and curious, and can you translate ecological expertise into successful designs of biodiverse, climate-resilient, aesthetically attractive and multifunctional green facades? Do you enjoy bridging fundamental ecological knowledge with practical applications? Then Wageningen University & Research offers an exciting opportunity for you. 
BIO-SKIN (Bio-Inspired Outer Surfaces to Kool, Insulate and Nurture) is developing bio-based, waste-derived, and circular façade systems that integrate plant growth. The project goal is to help bio-based facade panels that keep buildings cool, insulate, support biodiversity, and contribute to more sustainable urban environments. We work in a team of people with backgrounds in design, materials, biomaterial chemistry, architecture, biology, engineering, sustainability, and the built environment.
In this position, you will investigate how plant-soil-insect interactions develop in ecosystems with shallow soils and translate these ecological insights into design principles for next-generation green façades. Your research will contribute to a better understanding of how ecological communities establish and function in constrained urban environments, while helping to develop façade systems that support biodiversity and ecosystem functioning.
As a PhD candidate, you will combine fundamental and applied research to develop innovative green façade concepts that enhance ecosystem complexity and deliver key ecosystem services, including thermal insulation, carbon sequestration, microclimate regulation, and habitat provision for insects and other arthropods. This involves designing and setting up mini-ecosystems in minimal soil/vertical environments at various Living/Field Lab locations, and monitoring their performance, biodiversity and impact for energy efficiency. You will design the façade-panel experiments in close collaboration with a postdoctoral researcher, analyse ecological and physiological data, and contribute to scientific publications.
The project offers a unique opportunity to connect ecology, ecophysiology, urban greening, and green façade design.
We are looking for a candidate who enjoys working in interdisciplinary teams. You will bring strong botanical expertise to a collaborative group of researchers, designers, and material developers, and partners from companies that produce green façades, jointly creating innovative green façade solutions that contribute to sustainable construction and healthier urban environments.
Your activities include:
 Investigating plant species performance, community assembly and plant-insect-soil interactions in shallow-substrate systems (drawing on insights from literature as well as field studies);
 Year-round monitoring at various Living/Field Lab locations on the impact of plant species for enhancing energy efficiency and biodiversity by green façade panels;
 Analysing ecological and ecophysiological datasets;
 Publishing results in peer-reviewed journals and presenting findings at scientific conferences;
 Collaborating with academic and non-academic partners to translate scientific insights into practical applications;
 Teaching in courses and supervise BSc and MSc students in biodiversity-themed research.
 You will work here 
The research is embedded within the Biosystematics Group and the Laboratory of Entomology You will be supervised by dr. ir. Casper Quist and Prof. Bregje Wertheim . As a member in the BIO-SKIN team you will work one day a week together with the other BIO-SKIN PhDs and Post-docs at the AMS institute in Amsterdam . In addition, you will be embedded in the PE&RC graduate school ( Home | PE&RC ), which will allow you to follow a wide variety of training courses and provide support during your academic journey.

REQUIREMENTS:
For this project, we are looking for an enthusiastic, highly motivated and curious PhD candidate, who can translate botanical and ecological expertise into successful designs of biodiverse, climate-resilient, aesthetically attractive and multifunctional green facades.
 You have or are: 
 A successfully completed MSc degree in forest- and nature conservation or biology
 Extensive knowledge of the Dutch flora, able to accurately identify plant species in the field
 A strong interest in ecological interactions, including relationships between plants, insects, and soil organisms
 Interest in and initial experience with interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary collaboration, and the ability to engage with stakeholders from diverse backgrounds, including design, engineering, education, and ecology.
 Excellent communication skills in Dutch and English and experience with teaching and scientific writing.
For this position your command of the English and Dutch language is expected to be at C1 level . Sometimes it is necessary to submit an internationally recognised Certificate of Proficiency in the English Language. More information can be found here .

CONTRACT: 18 months

The Copernicus Institute of Sustainable Development at Utrecht University invites applications for a PhD position on the role of art-science-action integration and challenge-based learning towards transformative sustainability education. 
 Your job
 The PhD candidate will investigate how higher education can prepare students to have meaningful contributions in complex sustainability challenges. Specifically, the PhD candidate will study how the integration of academic knowledge, the skills to make academic knowledge actionable in these complex challenges, and the use of artistic expressions can strengthen students’ professional impact. 
 A specific focus in the research lies on challenge-based learning environments, in which students from different disciplinary backgrounds work with educators, artists and societal partners on real-world sustainability issues. Situated at the intersection of sustainability education, transformative learning, challenge-based learning and arts-based interventions, the project combines scientific ambitions with the wish of the research having impact within Utrecht University and beyond. It aims to advance knowledge on transformative sustainability education while contributing to the development of effective and inclusive educational practices.
 Your role and research 
As a PhD candidate, you will develop and carry out an independent research programme within a broader project. Together with an interdisciplinary supervisory team and a range of academic and societal partners, you will explore how knowledge, skills and artistic expression can be combined to support sustainability learning and help students engage with complex sustainability challenges. Your research may address questions such as:
 How can artistic practices contribute to cognitive, affective and action-oriented sustainability learning?
 How can challenge-based education connect disciplinary knowledge with the experiences and priorities of societal partners?
 What opportunities and tensions arise when artists, scientists, educators and societal actors collaborate?
 How can skills be taught so that they enable action in practice?
 What are the (educational or institutional) conditions that enable art-science collaborations that can have a real impact on student learning?
 Your work will include designing and conducting empirical research in higher-education settings, analysing qualitative and/or quantitative data, and translating findings into both academic and practical outputs. Possible methods include interviews, surveys, observations, focus groups and the analysis of student work. The precise research questions and methodological approach will be developed together with the supervisory team.
 You will also contribute to the evaluation and further development of sustainability skills and challenge-based courses, and help strengthen collaboration between educators, students, artists and societal partners. You will have opportunities to share your findings at conferences and workshops and to publish in international peer-reviewed journals. As part of the Copernicus Institute research community, you will also participate in relevant doctoral training activities.
 Your qualities
 We are looking for a curious, motivated and collaborative researcher with a strong interest in the role of higher education in sustainability transformation.
 You have:
 a completed Master’s degree in sustainability science, environmental sciences, educational sciences, social sciences, governance, transformation studies, arts-based research, or a related field;
 a clear interest in sustainability education, transformative learning, challenge-based learning, art-science collaboration or related topics;
 strong analytical, academic writing and communication skills;
 experience with qualitative and/or quantitative research methods;
 the ability to work independently and collaboratively in a multidisciplinary environment.
 Experience with educational research, stakeholder engagement, arts-based methods or mixed-methods research is an advantage, but is not required. Being able to collect data (using interviews or surveys) using the Dutch language is also an advantage. We welcome applicants with diverse disciplinary and professional backgrounds who can demonstrate a strong fit with the research topic.
 Our offer
 You will join the Copernicus Institute of Sustainable Development, an interdisciplinary research environment addressing urgent sustainability challenges through research, education and societal engagement. You will receive supervision from an interdisciplinary team and have opportunities to participate in doctoral training, seminars, conferences and international research networks.
 We offer
 a position (0.8 - 1.0 FTE) for 1 year, with an extension to a total of four years upon a successful assessment in the first year, and with the specific intent that it results in a doctorate within this period;
 a working week of 32 - 40 hours and a gross monthly salary between €3.204 and €4.051 (salary scale P under the Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Universities (CAO NU)). The salary is based on a 38-hour working week;
 8% holiday pay and 8.3% year-end bonus;

As a postdoctoral researcher you will be addressing pressing questions of urban inclusion, health inequalities and social justice. You will join an ambitious and international team, and you will be offered opportunities for international collaboration, academic publishing, conference participation and meaningful engagement with policymakers and community organisations. 
Radboud University is seeking a motivated postdoctoral researcher to join the European DUT research project TOILED ( Towards More Resilient Urban Infrastructures through Toilet-Led Research and Policy on Provisioning, Accessibility and Maintenance of Public Toilets ). The project is coordinated by Dr Rianne van Melik and brings together researchers and urban partners from the Netherlands, Belgium and Türkiye. Project outputs include academic articles, city reports, policy briefs and a Toilet Manifesto. Join us in challenging the neglect of sanitation in urban research and policy, and help shape more inclusive cities for all.
Public toilets are essential yet often overlooked urban infrastructures. They shape who can access and participate in urban life, particularly older adults, people experiencing homelessness, people with disabilities, and people with digestive illnesses. TOILED aims to understand how more resilient, inclusive and equitable cities can be created through improved public toilet governance. The project investigates three interrelated themes: provisioning, socio-spatial accessibility and maintenance of public toilets in Rotterdam (Netherlands), Ghent (Belgium) and Ankara (Türkiye).
As a postdoctoral researcher, you will play a central role in the project. You will contribute to the design and coordination of comparative research across the three cities and conduct fieldwork in Rotterdam. The project employs a qualitative and interdisciplinary methodology, including policy and institutional analysis, mapping exercises, ethnographic observations and interviews with policymakers, toilet providers, maintenance workers, advocacy organisations and particular populations that need toilets more than others (older adults, homeless individuals, disabled people, and people with digestive illnesses).
You will collaborate closely with international academic partners at the University of Antwerp and Middle East Technical University, as well as with municipal authorities (those of Rotterdam in particular) and civil-society stakeholders. Together, the consortium seeks to generate new knowledge on urban inequalities, social infrastructure and public space, while translating research findings into practical recommendations for policy and practice.

REQUIREMENTS:
You hold a PhD in Human Geography, Urban Studies, Urban Sociology, Spatial Planning or a related discipline.
 You have proven interests in and knowledge of theories on public space, social infrastructure, social inclusion and/or diversity, and preferably an affinity for public toilets as a research topic.
 You have experience with qualitative and/or ethnographic research methods.
 You can demonstrate an excellent academic publication record relative to your career stage.
 You have strong organisational and communication skills and proficiency in both English and Dutch (to conduct empirical research in Rotterdam).
 You are interested in co-creation, stakeholder engagement and policy-relevant research.
 You can work independently and collaboratively in an international research team.
 You have good skills in project planning.

Join Us! 
 A fully funded four-year Ph.D. position is available in the Complex Cyber Infrastructure research group at the University of Amsterdam. 
 As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes deeply embedded in our society, the urgency to warrant its responsible and accountable use is increasing. Examples include the control that creative industry actors need to manifest when using AI pipelines in the (moving) image industry. 
 This PhD project aims to focus on the emerging field of Accountable and Responsible AI, with the goal of advancing knowledge and practice at the intersection of AI research, creative industry practices, and societal regulatory expectations. Two projects underpin this position: SafeGenAI – a creative industry endeavour to enable creative industry actors to safely use GenAI tools; and LLM4LM – a large consortium addressing the legal-tech challenges in cross-organisational multi-domain agentic solutions. The candidate will not only have a chance to contribute to shaping the next generation AI systems within the creative industry and logistics practices, but also potentially to design more transparent, fair, and compliant ones with evolving societal and regulatory expectations. 
 The successful candidate will be embedded in a team that will help transfer fundamental research results into the creative industry and legal practices, respectively. Moreover, they will be working closely with the supervision team, as well as the other PhD students and postdocs in the research group. 
 This is what you will do 
 In this context, you will investigate the following key challenges: 
 Opacity in GenAI inferencing : How can the inferencing and reasoning processes of GenAI systems be made sufficiently transparent and traceable to support accountability in high-stakes professional contexts? 
 AI legal compliance-by-design : How can GenAI systems be built to satisfy the requirements of the regulations such as the EU AI Act — including transparency, human oversight, and risk management — while remaining practically useful in domain-specific workflows? 
 SMEs lack the expertise to navigate complex regulatory environments : How can domain-specific structured knowledge be integrated into GenAI systems to ground their outputs, reduce hallucination, and support trustworthy decision for non-expert users? 
 What we ask of you 
 Your experience and profile: 
 MSc in CS, AI or a closely related field. 
 Strong interest in Interest in finance and financial services is a plus.; previous experience in these fields is a plus. 
 Enthusiasm for the research process: studying research papers, solving complex problems, applying creative thinking, evaluation, reflection and disseminating findings via writing and oral presentations. 
 The ability to critically analyse abstract models as well as concrete implementations. 
 The ability to work individually as well as effectively in a team 
 Fluency in written and spoken English 
 This is what we offer you 
 A temporary contract for 38 hours per week for the duration of 4 years (the initial contract will be for a period of 18 months and after satisfactory evaluation it will be extended for a total duration of 4 years). The preferred starting date is as soon as possible. This should lead to a dissertation (PhD thesis). We will draft an educational plan that includes attendance of courses and (international) meetings. We also expect you to assist in teaching undergraduates and master students. 
 The gross monthly salary, based on 38 hours per week and dependent on relevant experience, ranges between € 3,204 to € 4,051 (scale P). This does not include 8% holiday allowance and 8,3% year-end allowance. The UFO profile PhD Candidate is applicable.. A favourable tax agreement, the ‘30% ruling’, may apply to non-Dutch applicants. The  Collective Labour Agreement of Universities of the Netherlands is applicable. 
 We also have an extensive secondary benefits package.  
 You will work in this team 
 The  Faculty of Science has a student body of around 8,000, as well as 1,800 members of staff working in education, research or support services. Researchers and students at the Faculty of Science are fascinated by every aspect of how the world works, be it elementary particles, the birth of the universe or the functioning of the brain. 
 The mission of the Informatics Institute (IvI) is to perform curiosity-driven and use-inspired fundamental research in Computer Science. The main research themes are Artificial Intelligence, Computational Science and Systems and Network Engineering. Our research involves complex information systems at large, with a focus on collaborative, data driven, computational and intelligent systems, all with a strong interactive component. 
 The Complex Cyber Infrastructure (CCI) group is part of the Informatics Institute at the University of Amsterdam. CCI focuses on the complexity of human-made systems on all scales. Cyber Infrastructure is rapidly evolving from relatively simple fixed components to programmable and virtualized objects with many degrees of freedom, owned, operated and governed by different entities in multiple administrative domains interacting on the Internet. Harnessing this complexity in a transparent, trustable way for safe and secure data processing is a major research topic that defines the focus of CCI research. The challenges are addressed by combining methods and results from research into sustainable and sovereign distributed data processing, programmable networks, policy reasoning and normative control, and software (language) engineering. 
 Want to know more about our organisation? Read more about   working at the University of Amsterdam.
